title: Selenium Nanoparticles Functionalized with Tumor-Targeting Peptides for Lung Cancer Therapy: A Comprehensive Review.
authors: Turk A, Mishra M, Kasana V et al.
abstract: Lung cancer is among the most fatal malignancies worldwide, with approximately 85% of diagnosed cases being non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite the considerable progress in surgical, chemotherapeutic, radiotherapeutic, and immunological treatments, the prognosis of NSCLC remains poor due to late-stage diagnosis, molecular heterogeneity, treatment resistance, recurrence, and systemic toxicity. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop more effective and less toxic therapies, and cancer nanotechnology has emerged as a promising approach. Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) are a viable option for lung cancer treatment because of their unique physicochemical and biochemical properties. They can be used for targeted drug delivery into cancer cells, as selenium possesses inherent anti-cancer properties, such as the induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial disruption, DNA damage, cell-cycle arrest, and modulation of several signaling pathways, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-κβ, STAT3, and p53, leading to cancer cell death and repression of tumor progression. Green synthesis of SeNPs using plant-derived phytochemicals is a sustainable strategy as it allows for simultaneous reduction and stabilization of nanoparticles, with an additional therapeutic phytochemical effect against cancer. Various phytochemicals, such as flavonoids, polyphenols, terpenoids, and alkaloids, have the ability to chelate metal ions and act as reducing agents and stabilizers in the synthesis of SeNPs. The antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and anti-metastatic activities of phytochemicals, along with their ability to inhibit the overexpressed enzymes, e.g., matrix metalloproteinases, in cancer cells, could provide an additional therapeutic benefit. However, the application of SeNPs in practice is limited by their low targeting ability, which results in poor bioavailability due to fast clearance from the bloodstream, reduced tumor accumulation, and poor cellular uptake. Conjugation of SeNPs with tumor-targeting peptides could enhance their delivery into the cancer cells. There is a variety of cell surface receptors that are overexpressed in lung cancer cells and can be used for targeted drug delivery. The most common receptors are EGFR, integrins, gastrin-releasing peptide receptor, neuropilin-1, and transferrin receptor. The ligands for these receptors, including the GE11 peptide for EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), RGD for integrins, bombesin for GRPR, and iRGD for neuropilin-1, could be used for targeting, as well as cell-penetrating peptides, such as TAT. This review discusses the current knowledge on the application of functionalized SeNPs for lung cancer treatment, specifically synthetic methods, physicochemical properties, mechanisms of action, and targeting strategies. Particular attention is paid to the combination of the anti-cancer effects of selenium and phytochemicals and their synergistic impact on tumor cell death. In addition, the challenges of the application of SeNPs for lung cancer treatment and possible future developments for functionalized SeNPs as novel therapeutic nanocarriers are discussed.

title: Population-Specific Pharmacogenetic Variants Associated with Chemotherapy Response in the Bulgarian Population.
authors: Miteva-Marcheva N, Ivanov H, Sotkova-Ivanova I et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pharmacogenetic variability influences the efficacy and toxicity of anticancer therapies. However, Eastern European populations remain underrepresented in pharmacogenetic databases. This study aimed to characterize pharmacogenetic variants relevant to chemotherapy response in the Bulgarian population and compare their allele frequencies with reference populations. Methods: Ninety individuals were included, comprising 50 patients with colorectal, non-small cell lung, or breast cancer and 40 healthy controls. Genomic DNA and circulating cell-free DNA were analyzed by next-generation sequencing targeting pharmacogenetic genes involved in drug metabolism, transport, and DNA repair. Allele frequencies were compared with gnomAD v2.1.1 reference data. Sensitivity analyses compared Bulgarian controls with Bulgarian non-cancer and combined Southern European, Northwestern European, and Other non-Finnish European non-cancer populations. Results: Twenty-three pharmacogenetic variants were evaluated. Six variants remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction in both Fisher's exact test and the two-proportion Z-test. Five variants-DPYD c.2194G>A, XPC c.2815C>A, EGFR c.1562G>A, XRCC1 c.1196A>G, and ERCC2 c.2251A>C-showed higher allele frequencies, whereas ERCC2 c.934G>A was less frequent in the Bulgarian cohort. DPYD c.85T>C remained significant after correction in the Z-test but not in Fisher's exact test. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the significance of XPC c.2815C>A in both reference-population comparisons, while DPYD c.85T>C remained significant only against the combined European reference population. Conclusions: Several pharmacogenetic variants showed distinct allele frequencies in the Bulgarian cohort. XPC c.2815C>A demonstrated the most robust population-specific pattern across sensitivity analyses. These findings highlight the value of locally derived pharmacogenetic data for precision oncology and pharmacogenetically guided treatment strategies.

title: Osimertinib Optimal Dosing Through Population Pharmacokinetics in Virtual Patients with NSCLC: An Approach Integrating Multiple Studies.
authors: Lim JW, Kim H, Lee H et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Osimertinib is a third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) T790M mutations in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). A comprehensive population pharmacokinetic (popPK) model may inform dosing across patient populations. The objective was to develop an integrated popPK model for osimertinib in virtual patients with NSCLC and to evaluate the influence of patient characteristics on PK variability. Methods: Data were extracted from four published popPK studies of osimertinib in patients with NSCLC. A virtual cohort of 1000 patients from each study was simulated using the corresponding final popPK model, with covariate distributions reconstructed from the reported demographics, resulting in a total virtual cohort of 4000 patients. The primary outcome was the development of a popPK model using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. Demographic and clinical covariates were evaluated for effects on PK variability. Results: A parent-metabolite one-compartment model best described osimertinib popPK. Body weight and serum albumin were significant covariates, with lower body weight and lower albumin concentrations associated with increased osimertinib plasma exposure. However, simulations demonstrated that the standard 80 mg once-daily dose maintained plasma concentrations within the literature-informed reference interval across all body weight and albumin subgroups. Conclusions: This popPK model suggests that despite significant effects of body weight and albumin on osimertinib exposure, routine dose adjustment may not be required. The standard 80 mg once-daily regimen maintains concentrations within the reference interval across diverse virtual patient populations with NSCLC, supporting current dosing recommendations. These model-informed findings warrant prospective validation with real-world clinical data to confirm generalizability.

title: ADAM10 as a Potential Biomarker in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer and Its Major Histologic Subtypes.
authors: Kim SB, Kim YJ, Lee Y et al.
abstract: Background and Objectives: A disintegrin and metalloproteinase 10 (ADAM10) is a membrane-anchored metalloprotease involved in ectodomain shedding and cancer progression. However, its molecular and prognostic significance across major histological subtypes of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains unclear. This study evaluated the clinical and molecular relevance of ADAM10 in NSCLC, focusing on lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC). Materials and Methods: Transcriptomic and clinicopathological data from 980 patients with NSCLC, including 491 patients with LUAD and 489 patients with LUSC, were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas through the OncoLnc database. Patients in each cohort were classified into ADAM10-high and ADAM10-low groups according to the median ADAM10 mRNA expression level. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to evaluate the prognostic significance of ADAM10 expression. Results: ADAM10 expression was not significantly associated with baseline clinicopathological characteristics in the overall cohort or within the LUAD and LUSC subgroups. However, ADAM10 expression showed distinct molecular associations according to histologic subtype. In LUAD, ADAM10 expression was positively correlated with KRAS expression (ρ = 0.286, p < 0.001), BRAF expression (ρ = 0.145, p = 0.001), and EGFR expression (ρ = 0.187, p < 0.001), while it was negatively correlated with TP53 expression (ρ = -0.12, p = 0.005), whereas in LUSC, it was positively correlated with PIK3CA. High ADAM10 expression was associated with significantly poorer EFS and OS in the overall NSCLC cohort. In multivariate analyses, high ADAM10 expression remained an independent predictor of shorter EFS (HR = 1.352, 95% CI = 1.041-1.755, p = 0.024) and OS (HR = 1.335, 95% CI = 1.089-1.636, p = 0.005), independent of clinicopathological factors. Conclusions: High ADAM10 expression was independently associated with poorer survival outcomes in NSCLC, with a more pronounced prognostic impact in LUAD than in LUSC. These findings suggest that ADAM10 may serve as a potential prognostic biomarker in NSCLC, particularly in LUAD.

title: Green Micelle-Enhanced Spectrofluorimetric Determination of Gefitinib in Pharmaceutical Tablets Using Cremophor RH 40: Response-Surface Optimization and Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TD-DFT) Interpretation.
authors: Bakheit AH, Alzaid AMA, Almajed AA
abstract: Gefitinib is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor used in non-small-cell lung cancer. This study developed a micelle-enhanced spectrofluorimetric method for its determination in tablets using native fluorescence and Cremophor RH 40 without derivatization. Experimental conditions were screened by a univariate approach and further evaluated by response-surface methodology. The quadratic model was significant (F = 83.26, p = 0.0019), and three confirmation experiments yielded prediction errors of 0.515-0.954%, supporting local agreement at the selected conditions. Fluorescence intensity was measured at an emission wavelength of 394 nm following excitation at 333 nm. The method was linear over 50-1200 ng mL-1 (r = 0.9997). The calculated limits of detection and quantification were 6.89 and 20.89 ng mL-1, respectively, while 50 ng mL-1 was retained as the lowest validated concentration. The method showed acceptable accuracy, repeatability, and selectivity for the investigated tablet matrix. Robustness testing indicated that pH requires careful control around 8.0. Analysis of pooled commercial tablets yielded an assay of 100.21 ± 1.86% of the label claim. TD-DFT calculations supported qualitative interpretation of the electronic transitions. The AGREE score was 0.61, indicating a more favorable environmental profile than the reference spectrofluorimetric method comparator (0.46).

title: Ommaya Reservoir-Based Cerebrospinal Fluid Chemotherapy for Leptomeningeal Metastasis in the Era of Targeted Therapy: Safety, Survival, and Exploratory Prognostic Factors from a Single-Center Cohort.
authors: Li H, Cai H, Lu X et al.
abstract: Objective: Real-world data on Ommaya reservoir-based cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) chemotherapy for leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) in the targeted-therapy era are limited. We describe its safety and survival and explore prognostic factors in lung adenocarcinoma-associated LM. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 68 patients with LM treated with Ommaya reservoir implantation and CSF chemotherapy. Overall survival (OS) was estimated from LM diagnosis and from implantation, and an exploratory multivariable Cox regression was performed in patients with actionable driver mutations receiving targeted therapy. Results: Device-related complications occurred in six patients (8.8%), including three catheter malpositions after freehand placement; chemotherapy-related adverse effects occurred in four (5.9%). After a median follow-up of 12.8 months, 14 patients (20.6%) had died, 10 of CNS progression. Median OS was not reached from diagnosis (24-month OS 67.8%) and 18.7 months from implantation (24-month OS 48.3%). In the exploratory analysis (n = 46), KPS, age, and EGFR mutation subtype were associated with OS from both time origins. Conclusions: Ommaya reservoir-based CSF chemotherapy was feasible with few device-related complications. Because all patients were treated and most had lung adenocarcinoma receiving targeted therapy, the favorable survival cannot be attributed to the reservoir or generalized to other primary tumors; prognostic factors require prospective validation.

title: Association of HBsAg Positivity and HBV Reactivation in EGFR-Mutant Lung Adenocarcinoma Treated with EGFR-TKIs: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Sun J, Lin J, Li H et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: EGFR-TKIs serve as standard first-line targeted therapy for EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Real-world data on the prognostic role of baseline HBsAg positivity and the risk of HBV reactivation during EGFR-TKI treatment remain limited, particularly in HBV-endemic Chinese populations.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort study enrolled 580 consecutive patients with stage III-IV EGFR-mutant LUAD who received EGFR-TKIs between 2013 and 2026. Patients were grouped by baseline HBsAg status; Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox models adjusted for key clinical covariates were used to evaluate progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). HBV reactivation was defined by EASL criteria, with virological evaluation available for 51 of 82 HBsAg-positive patients.
RESULTS: Among all enrolled patients, 14.1% were HBsAg-positive. The HBV reactivation rate was 9.8% among evaluable HBsAg-positive patients, and reactivation was not independently linked to survival. After adjustment, baseline HBsAg positivity showed a borderline trend toward poorer OS (HR = 1.42, 95% CI, 0.99-2.04, p = 0.054) without significant PFS association (HR = 1.14, 95% CI, 0.80-1.62, p = 0.481). Liver metastasis independently predicted worse OS in HBsAg-positive patients (HR = 3.84, 95% CI, 1.65-8.94, p = 0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: HBV reactivation was uncommon but warrants close monitoring during EGFR-TKI therapy. Baseline HBsAg positivity demonstrated only a non-significant trend toward inferior OS without affecting PFS. Routine HBsAg screening at diagnosis may facilitate risk stratification, and HBsAg-positive patients with liver metastasis require intensified surveillance.

title: Real-World Utilization of Tissue-Free ctDNA MRD Testing in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Across Asia-Pacific and the Middle East: A Descriptive Cohort Analysis and Illustrative Case Series.
authors: Lee CH, Jain S, Chen LC et al.
abstract: Introduction: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based molecular residual disease (MRD) testing is emerging as a tool to refine relapse risk and guide surveillance after curative-intent therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Tissue-free (plasma-only) MRD assays may improve feasibility where tumor tissue is limited. Prospective and trial-embedded studies have established that ctDNA MRD detected after curative-intent therapy is prognostic for recurrence in NSCLC, but how tissue-free MRD testing is deployed in routine care in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East (AMEA) has not been described. We characterized ordering patterns and first-test positivity in an AMEA cohort. In this descriptive cohort (159 NSCLC patients; 257 samples), 40.9% of patients underwent more than one MRD test, with a median interval of 4.9 months between the first two tests; first-test MRD positivity was 15.7% (25/159; 95% CI 10.9-22.2) with rates of 0% (0/9; 95% CI 0.0-29.9), 8.8% (5/57; 95% CI 3.8-18.9), 21.5% (17/79; 95% CI 13.9-31.8) and 21.4% (3/14; 95% CI 7.6-47.6), respectively, across stages I, II, III, and oligometastatic stage IV disease. No hypothesis testing was performed, and the stage I and oligometastatic stage IV subgroups are small, so the confidence intervals overlap widely and apparent between-stage differences should not be interpreted as a stage effect. Case Presentation: Six illustrative cases involving patients with stage II-IVB describe the use of MRD testing in routine clinical care. The cases were selected purposively, not consecutively, to span the contexts in which the results were interpreted: a positive result shortly before radiographic nodal recurrence (Case 1); a positive result during long-term adjuvant osimertinib preceding isolated mediastinal relapse (Case 2); a transient positive result with subsequent clearance and radiographic regression (Case 3); a positive result that prompted PET-CT revealing occult metastatic disease (Case 4); serially negative results concordant with sustained radiographic remission (Case 5); and a positive result that prompted comprehensive genomic profiling identifying an actionable KRAS G12C alteration (Case 6). Conclusions: Across Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, tissue-free MRD testing in NSCLC was used primarily during surveillance and often serially; first-test positivity was 15.7% (95% CI 10.9-22.2) overall, with wide and mutually overlapping confidence intervals across stages. The cases illustrate that MRD results may prompt diagnostic evaluation when interpreted alongside imaging and other clinical findings, but they are purposively selected, and treatment changes that followed a result are reported as description, not as evidence of benefit. No assay performance characteristic is estimated. These findings are hypothesis-generating; prospective, MRD-directed trials with standardized timepoints, thresholds, confirmatory strategies and pre-specified clinical actions are needed before MRD results can guide treatment.

title: Clinical Utility of Broad-Panel Profiling in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Pairwise Co-Mutational Gene Patterns and PD-L1 Associations Define Stage-Specific Prognosis.
authors: Sassorossi C, De Paolis E, Evangelista J et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Precision medicine has improved outcomes in advanced lung cancer, but its implementation remains limited. The prospective LANTERN project (NCT05802771) involves comprehensive clinical and multi-omics data collection. Here, we report preliminary genomic findings, focusing on the prognostic impact of gene mutations, pairwise co-mutational patterns, and their stage-specific association with PD-L1 analysis on patients speciments.
METHODS: This prospective, multicenter observational study enrolled 271 consecutive patients between March 2023 and December 2024, including 137 with stage I-III and 134 with stage IV disease. Comprehensive genomic profiling was performed using the TruSight Oncology 500 High Throughput assay to assess single nucleotide variants, insertions/deletions, copy number alterations, tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability. The prognostic role of mutations and co-mutations was evaluated, together with associations between genomic alterations and PD-L1 expression.
RESULTS: At least one Tier I-II alteration was identified in 84% of patients. TP53 (39%), KRAS (27%), EGFR (15%), and STK11 (11%) were the most frequently altered genes. Several co-mutations were associated with worse overall survival, including TP53/STK11, STK11/LRP1B, STK11/RB1 and RB1/LRP1B, and with reduced disease-free survival, particularly TP53/KRAS, TP53/STK11, KRAS/STK11 and STK11/LRP1B. In advanced disease, STK11 and KEAP1 mutations were associated with low PD-L1 expression, whereas PIK3CA, PTEN and ARID1A mutations correlated with higher PD-L1 expression in early-stage tumors.
CONCLUSIONS: Comprehensive genomic profiling reveals substantial molecular heterogeneity across lung cancer stages and identifies co-mutational patterns with prognostic and immune-related relevance, supporting broader molecular testing at diagnosis.

title: Efficacy Augmentation of Ferroptosis-Inducing Nanomedicine for Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor-Resistant Lung Cancer Brain Metastasis.
authors: Zeng Y, Lin C, Yang J et al.
abstract: Acquired resistance to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) poses a major clinical challenge for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer patients with brain metastasis. A key unresolved question is whether the adaptive mechanisms driving TKI resistance also confer new therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we reveal that TKI-resistant lung cancer brain metastatic cells develop a redox perturbation state, characterized by elevated oxidative stress and diminished antioxidant capacity, which confers a latent sensitivity to ferroptosis induction. To exploit this vulnerability, we developed MIL-S@M, a brain-targeted nanoplatform capable of efficient blood-brain barrier penetration and glutathione-responsive drug release. MIL-S@M potently induces ferroptosis through the synergistic effects of iron overload, glutathione depletion, and glutathione peroxidase 4 inactivation. In mouse models of osimertinib-resistant brain metastasis, MIL-S@M significantly suppressed tumor growth and extended survival, both as a monotherapy and in combination with osimertinib, without inducing systemic or neurotoxic effects. This work unveils a targetable adaptation in TKI-resistant brain metastasis and presents a translatable nanotherapeutic strategy.

title: Previously Unrecognized Distinct Laryngeal Lesions During Lazertinib Therapy in EGFR-Mutated NSCLC: A Case Series.
authors: Kang SH, Kim H, Ji JY et al.
abstract: Lazertinib (LECLAZA®) is a third-generation epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), especially in patients with brain metastases. While common adverse events such as rash and pruritus have been reported, voice-related complications and structural laryngeal lesions have not previously been reported. Here, we describe four NSCLC patients who developed new-onset voice changes or globus sensation during lazertinib-based therapy. Laryngoscopic examination revealed multifocal, broad-based polypoid mucosal thickening that was atypical for benign conditions such as contact granuloma or reflux-related disease. Histopathology in one patient demonstrated benign inflamed granulation tissue, and all lesions remained stable without interval progression over 15-36 months of follow-up. Given the small number of cases and the potential confounders, a causal association with lazertinib cannot be established. However, awareness of these benign-appearing mucosal findings may help clinicians avoid unnecessary biopsy or interruption of cancer treatment when evaluating throat or voice symptoms in patients receiving lazertinib therapy.

title: Lung Cancer Spectrum, Molecular Alterations and PD-L1 Expression.
authors: Fatima A, Redmond M
abstract:
AIM: This audit evaluated lung cancer cases diagnosed in 2024, focusing on histological subtypes, molecular testing, and PD-L1 expression to assess diagnostic trends and biomarker testing compliance.
METHODS: All lung malignancy cases on core biopsy or cytology between January 1 and December 31, 2024, were included. Data were extracted from the institutional lab information system (Win-Path and Power-chart).
RESULTS: Adenocarcinoma was the most common subtype, accounting for 91 (55%) cases, followed by squamous cell carcinoma 32 (19%) cases, small cell carcinoma, 17 (10%) cases, carcinoma NOS, 24 (14%) cases, and High-grade Neuroendocrine carcinoma, 1 (1%) case. Molecular testing was performed in 83 (50%) cases. Reflex testing by pathologists was done in 76 (92%) cases and testing was done on clinician's request in 7 (8%) cases. Mutations were identified in 38 (46%) cases of them. KRAS mutations were detected in 19 (50%), EGFR in 8 (21%), BRAF in 6 (16%), MET exon 14 skipping in 2 (5%), and PIK3CA in 3 (8%). PD-L1 immunohistochemistry was performed on 110 (66%) of total cases. Among these, the tumour proportion score was <1% in 50 (45.5%) cases, 1-49% in 28 (25.5%) cases, and ≥50% in 32 (29%) cases.
DISCUSSION: Adenocarcinoma predominated, KRAS was the most common driver mutation, and PD-L1 expression influenced treatment decisions, aligning with global trends in precision oncology.

title: Computational characterization of Paraphamide B as a potential EGFR-preferential dual EGFR/ALK-binding candidate for non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Raghuram A
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Acquired resistance to selective inhibitors remains a major limitation in EGFR- and ALK-driven non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Dual-target inhibition is a theoretically motivated strategy for addressing compensatory signaling between these pathways, but experimental kinase inhibition and cellular activity remain necessary to establish whether a computationally prioritized compound has biological activity. In this study, a multi-stage computational pipeline was used to identify candidate dual EGFR/ALK-binding molecules from the NPAtlas microbial natural product database, comprising 36,454 compounds. Drug-likeness and structural-alert filtering reduced this chemical space to 3912 compounds for virtual screening. Paraphamide B was prioritized based on its combined docking performance and predicted hinge-region interactions at Met769 of EGFR and Met1199 of ALK, with docking scores of - 9.0 and - 7.8 kcal/mol, respectively. Triplicate 200 ns molecular dynamics simulations were used to assess the reproducibility and persistence of ligand-protein interactions. MM-GBSA calculations yielded more favorable relative binding-energy estimates for EGFR (- 37.43 ± 4.82 kcal/mol) than for ALK (- 16.67 ± 1.55 kcal/mol). Conformational clustering and PCA-derived free-energy landscapes indicated that Paraphamide B-associated complexes sampled relatively confined conformational ensembles comparable to the reference inhibitor-bound systems. In silico ADMET profiling indicated favorable physicochemical and drug-likeness characteristics but also identified predicted CYP inhibition and toxicity liabilities requiring experimental assessment. DFT analysis characterized the electronic properties of Paraphamide B, including its electrophilicity and molecular electrostatic potential, providing physicochemical context for the predicted interaction geometry. Taken together, these results suggest that Paraphamide B may represent a promising computationally identified dual-target hit candidate, with an EGFR-preferential predicted interaction profile, warranting further experimental validation.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00777-3.

title: Chinese medicine combined with EGFR-TKIs in EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC: a meta-analysis of efficacy and safety.
authors: Li X, Qian D, Liu S et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: For advanced EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKI) therapy is the primary treatment, but drug resistance and side effects reduce its effectiveness. Integrating Chinese and Western medicine is a key focus in cancer treatment. This study evaluates the clinical benefits of combining traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) with EGFR-TKI, summarizing TCM syndromes and medication traits.
METHODS: We searched six databases for relevant clinical studies. A meta-analysis assessed progression-free survival (PFS), disease control rate (DCR), and adverse reactions, with subgroup analysis by EGFR mutation type. A TCM syndrome network was created to examine syndrome distribution and core prescription patterns.
RESULTS: TCM combined with EGFR-TKIs significantly improved PFS (HR = 0.70, 95%CI 0.65-0.76, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%), benefiting patients with Exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation equally (p = 0.75). The combination therapy increased DCR (RR = 1.19, 95% CI 1.01-1.40, p = 0.04), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 89%), and reduced targeted-agent-related adverse reactions. Qi-Yin and Lung-Spleen deficiency were the dominant TCM syndromes, managed via Qi-tonifying, Yin-nourishing and spleen-strengthening regimens.
CONCLUSION: Integrating TCM with EGFR-TKI enhances tumor control and treatment safety in advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations, showing consistent efficacy across various mutation types. This approach, which considers clinical syndrome differentiation and medication patterns in Chinese medicine, offers evidence-based guidance for personalized treatment. This review was performed following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261398486, identifier CRD420261398486.

title: EGFR-TKI-associated colitis in non-small cell lung cancer: a retrospective characterization of clinical, radiographic, endoscopic, and histopathologic features.
authors: Wang S, Tan C, Shi P et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard targeted therapies for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but clinically documented EGFR-TKI-associated colitis remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to describe its clinical, radiographic, endoscopic, histopathologic, management, and exploratory survival features.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective case-control analysis nested within an institutional cohort of 3,285 patients with NSCLC treated with EGFR-TKIs between January 2018 and July 2025. The analysis included 43 patients with documented radiographic and/or endoscopic colitis and 223 selected asymptomatic controls. Clinical, imaging, colonoscopic, histopathologic, treatment, and survival data were reviewed. Ever-smoking was examined in an exploratory univariable logistic analysis. Drug-specific EGFR-TKI odds were not estimated because a common time-aligned exposure definition for cases and controls could not be reconstructed, and overall survival was examined exploratorily.
RESULTS: Clinically documented EGFR-TKI-associated colitis occurred in 43/3,285 treated patients (1.3%). Ever-smoking was more frequent among cases than selected controls (39.5% vs. 20.2%; univariable odds ratio = 2.586, 95% confidence interval: 1.293-5.173, P = 0.007). Drug-specific odds were not estimated because a common time-aligned exposure definition could not be reconstructed. Median symptom onset was 3 months. Diarrhea occurred in 40/43 patients (93.0%); three patients had grade 0 diarrhea. Among 39 patients undergoing colonoscopy, 14 had normal-appearing mucosa; 11 of these patients underwent biopsy and showed histologic inflammation. Of 35 classifiable biopsies, 10 (28.6%) showed a microscopic pattern, 14 (40.0%) an inflammatory/IBD-like pattern, and 11 (31.4%) an ischemic-like pattern. In exploratory survival analysis, no statistically significant association between documented colitis and overall survival was detected (log-rank P = 0.538; adjusted HR = 1.184, 95% CI: 0.782-1.793, P = 0.426).
CONCLUSION: Clinically documented EGFR-TKI-associated colitis showed heterogeneous radiographic, endoscopic, and histopathologic patterns. Normal-appearing mucosa did not exclude histologic inflammation in biopsied patients. The 1.3% value represents documented cases in this institutional cohort rather than population incidence. The recorded smoking difference, severity-stratified findings, treatment outcomes, and survival estimates should be interpreted as exploratory; no drug-specific colitis association is inferred.

title: [Noninvasive prediction of EGFR gene mutation in lung adenocarcinoma using multiparametric CT perfusion imaging].
authors: Chen C, Liu X, Xie Q et al.
journal: Zhong Nan Da Xue Xue Bao Yi Xue Ban
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Determination of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation status is essential for molecular targeted therapy in patients with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Currently, tumor tissue for genetic testing is commonly obtained through invasive procedures such as surgery or needle biopsy. This study aims to explore the potential associations between multiple quantitative parameters derived from computed tomography perfusion imaging (CTPI) and EGFR gene mutations in patients with LUAD, and to provide preliminary evidence for the noninvasive prediction of EGFR mutation status in LUAD.
METHODS: Patients with LUAD pathologically confirmed by surgery or needle biopsy at The Third Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, were enrolled. All patients underwent pulmonary CTPI within 1 week before surgery and subsequently underwent EGFR gene testing. According to the EGFR gene testing results, the patients were divided into an EGFR-mutant group and an EGFR-wild-type group. Differences in CTPI-derived quantitative parameters between the 2 groups were statistically analyzed. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of EGFR mutation and to construct a combined prediction model. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under the curve (AUC) were used to evaluate the predictive performance of each independent predictor and the combined model.
RESULTS: A total of 82 patients were ultimately included, comprising 45 women and 37 men. EGFR mutations were detected in 46 patients, while 36 had wild-type EGFR. Blood volume (BV), time to peak (TTP), and capillary permeability surface (PS) were significantly higher in the EGFR-mutant group than in the wild-type group (5.38±1.57 vs 3.08±1.17, P<0.001; 28.02±5.07 vs 24.47±7.14, P=0.014; 18.90±7.24 vs 12.11±6.11, P<0.001, respectively). No statistically significant differences were observed between the 2 groups in blood flow (BF), mean transit time (MTT), time to maximum of the tissue residue function (Tmax), positive enhancement integral (PEI), or mean slope of increase (MSI) (all P>0.05). Among the parameters showing significant between-group differences, BV (P<0.001) and PS (P=0.002) were independent predictors of EGFR mutation. ROC curve analysis revealed that the AUCs of BV and PS were 0.885 and 0.760, respectively, with corresponding cutoff values of 3.81 mL/100 g and 16.20 mL/(min·100 g). The combined CTPI prediction model incorporating BV and PS achieved an AUC of 0.923, which was higher than that of either parameter alone (both P<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: The quantitative CTPI parameters BV and PS are independent predictors of EGFR mutation in patients with LUAD. The combined CTPI model incorporating BV and PS demonstrated good predictive potential in this cohort, although further validation in large, multicenter studies is required.

title: Izalontamab brengitecan versus platinum-based chemotherapy in EGFR-mutated advanced non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer after progression on third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (PANKU-Lung01): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial in China.
authors: Hong S, Zhou T, Hou X et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren) is a first-in-class bispecific antibody-drug conjugate targeting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 (HER3) and has shown antitumour activity in EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We compared iza-bren with platinum-based chemotherapy in participants with EGFR-mutated advanced non-squamous NSCLC after progression on third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
METHODS: In this multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial (PANKU-Lung01) conducted at 73 sites in China, eligible participants had EGFR-mutated locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC, disease progression after third-generation EGFR TKIs, and had received no previous chemotherapy for advanced disease. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive iza-bren (2·5 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 8 of each 3-week cycle) or pemetrexed plus carboplatin or cisplatin for four to six cycles, with pemetrexed maintenance permitted in participants without progression. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). The primary analysis included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of study treatment (modified intention-to-treat population). We report the prespecified final progression-free survival and interim overall survival analyses. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06382116.
FINDINGS: Between May 22, 2024, and Sept 1, 2025, we screened 654 participants. After 222 (34%) were excluded, 432 (66%) participants were randomly assigned to iza-bren (n=217 [50%]) or chemotherapy (n=215 [50%]); 422 (98%) received study treatment (216 [51%] in the iza-bren group and 206 [49%] in the chemotherapy group) and comprised the modified intention-to-treat population. At the data cutoff (July 15, 2026; median follow-up for progression-free survival 14·6 months [95% CI 12·9-16·7] in the iza-bren group vs 15·2 months [11·2-18·2] in the chemotherapy group), median BICR-assessed progression-free survival was 11·1 months (9·2-12·7) with iza-bren versus 5·7 months (5·5-5·9) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio [HR] 0·40 [95% CI 0·31-0·51]; one-sided p<0·0001). Treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse occurred in 170 (79%) of 216 participants in the iza-bren group and 128 (62%) of 206 in the chemotherapy group (predominantly haematological); treatment-related adverse events led to permanent discontinuation of at least one study-treatment component in four (2%) participants in each group and treatment-related deaths occurred in one participant in each group. Treatment-related interstitial lung disease occurred in two (1%) participants in the iza-bren group and none in the chemotherapy group.
INTERPRETATION: In participants with EGFR-mutated advanced non-squamous NSCLC after progression on third-generation EGFR TKIs, iza-bren significantly prolonged progression-free survival, although treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were more frequent than with chemotherapy. To our knowledge, these findings provide the first phase 3 evidence for a bispecific antibody-drug conjugate and support iza-bren as a potential treatment option in this population.

title: Ruzaltatug rezetecan versus chemotherapy for EGFR-mutated advanced non-small-cell lung cancer progressing after EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy (HERON-Lung01): interim analysis of a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial in China.
authors: Xu CR, Zhang Y, Lin G et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ruzaltatug rezetecan is a novel HER3-directed antibody-drug conjugate that has shown promising antitumour activity and manageable safety in pretreated EGFR-.mutated non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in a phase 1 trial. We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of ruzaltatug rezetecan with chemotherapy in patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC that had progressed after EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy.
METHODS: HERON-Lung01 is a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial conducted at 62 sites in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years, with locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC harbouring an EGFR activating mutation (exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation), and had progressed during or after EGFR-TKI therapy. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive ruzaltatug rezetecan 8·0 mg/kg or chemotherapy comprising pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 plus carboplatin (area under the curve 5) or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 for four cycles, followed by maintenance pemetrexed. All treatments were administered intravenously on day 1 of each 3-week cycle. Block randomisation was stratified by presence of brain metastases, EGFR mutation subtype, and use of a first-line third-generation EGFR-TKI. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), as assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR), in the intention-to-treat population. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06671379). Recruitment is complete, with the trial ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Nov 29, 2024, and Jan 29, 2026, 498 patients were randomly assigned to receive ruzaltatug rezetecan (n=250) or chemotherapy (n=248). The median age was 60·0 years (IQR 54·0-68·0); 276 (55%) patients were female and 222 (45%) male. At the prespecified interim PFS analysis, median follow-up was 7·7 months (95% CI 7·1-8·3). BICR-assessed PFS was significantly longer with ruzaltatug rezetecan than with chemotherapy (median 8·3 months vs 5·4 months; hazard ratio 0·47 [95% CI 0·36-0·60]; one-sided p<0·0001). Grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 101 (41%) of 248 patients receiving ruzaltatug rezetecan and 93 (39%) of 239 patients receiving chemotherapy, most commonly decreased neutrophil count (64 [26%] of 248 patients vs 46 [19%] of 239 patients), decreased white blood cell count (29 [12%] vs 29 [12%]), and anaemia (15 [6%] vs 26 [11%]). TRAEs led to treatment discontinuation in three (1%) patients in the ruzaltatug rezetecan group and three (1%) in the chemotherapy group. One death (unknown cause) in the ruzaltatug rezetecan group was considered by the investigator to be possibly treatment related.
INTERPRETATION: Ruzaltatug rezetecan significantly prolonged PFS compared with chemotherapy, with a manageable safety profile, in EGFR-TKI-resistant, EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC. These data support ruzaltatug rezetecan as a potential treatment option in this setting.

title: From single to dual targeting: Recent advances in EGFR-based dual inhibitors for cancer therapy.
authors: Yalcin ZS, Alagoz MA, Algul O
abstract: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose overexpression and activating mutations drive the pathogenesis of solid tumors, particularly non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). ATP-competitive EGFR inhibitors have progressed through four generations with considerable clinical success, yet their durability is limited by acquired mutations such as T790 M and C797S and by activation of compensatory signaling pathways. Dual-targeting inhibitors are single chemical entities designed to engage two distinct molecular targets simultaneously, generally constructed by conjugating, fusing or merging the pharmacophores of two established ligands. Conjugation offers synthetic flexibility but increases molecular size; fusion reduces molecular size at the cost of potential affinity loss; merging yields the most drug-like molecules but requires substantial pharmacophore overlap. EGFR-based dual inhibitors retain EGFR as the primary target and add a second oncogenic node such as HER2, VEGFR-2 or microtubules. The structural plasticity of the EGFR kinase domain, together with its well-characterized hinge, back-pocket and solvent-exposed regions, tolerates side-chain and linker modification and has made EGFR a favored scaffold for this approach. Clinically approved multi-targeting agents including vandetanib and neratinib provide proof of principle. Such molecules can simplify pharmacokinetics relative to drug combinations, although a single emergent mutation may abolish both activities and broader target coverage can reduce selectivity, so clinical superiority over combination regimens has to be demonstrated for each target pair. This review examines studies published between 2020 and 2026 on EGFR-based dual inhibitors spanning 26 secondary targets, addressing rational design, structure-activity relationships, receptor-ligand interaction profiles, and preclinical and clinical efficacy, and identifies the strategies most likely to resolve the current limitations of EGFR-centered multi-target therapy.

title: miR-221/222 Profiles in Small Extracellular Vesicles Derived from Gemcitabine-Sensitive and -Resistant A549 Cancer Stem-like Cell Spheroids: An In Vitro Study.
authors: Ghorbani A, Uysal O, Karacaoğlu D
abstract: Background: Gemcitabine is used in the treatment of human non-small cell lung cancer (hNSCLC), yet acquired resistance can limit therapeutic responses. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) have been implicated in chemoresistance-associated intercellular signaling. We profiled the miR-221/222 cluster and resistance-associated genes in cancer stem-like cells (CSLCs) and CSLC-derived sEV preparations from gemcitabine-sensitive and -resistant A549 models. Methods: Gemcitabine-resistant A549 cells and matched cancer stem-like cell (CSLC) and gemcitabine-resistant cancer stem-like cell (Gr-CSLC) populations were generated and characterized by flow cytometry, qRT-PCR, and immunofluorescence. sEV preparations derived from CSLC and Gr-CSLC spheroids were characterized for total protein content, EV-associated tetraspanins, and vesicular morphology. PKH26-associated fluorescence following exposure of A549 cells to labeled sEV preparations was also evaluated. The relative levels of sEV-associated miR-221/222 family members and the resistance-associated genes MDR1, ABCG2, and BCL2 were assessed by qRT-PCR. Results: Gr-CSLCs exhibited enhanced spheroid formation and increased MDR1 expression. Gr-CSLC-derived sEV preparations showed higher total protein content than CSLC-derived preparations. Bead-based flow cytometry demonstrated EV-associated CD9 and CD81 expression, while cryo-TEM revealed small, membrane-bound vesicular structures. PKH26-associated intracellular fluorescence was observed in A549 cells following exposure to labeled sEV preparations. Gr-CSLC-derived sEVs showed higher relative levels of miR-221-3p, miR-222-3p, and miR-222-5p than CSLC-derived sEVs, whereas miR-221-5p showed no significant difference. MDR1 and BCL2 also showed higher relative expression in Gr-CSLC-derived sEVs, whereas ABCG2 showed no significant difference. Conclusions: sEV preparations derived from gemcitabine-resistant Gr-CSLCs exhibited distinct miR-221/222 and resistance-associated RNA profiles compared with those derived from gemcitabine-sensitive CSLCs in this in vitro A549 NSCLC model. These molecular differences should be interpreted as associations with the resistant phenotype rather than evidence of functional transfer of chemoresistance. Further functional studies and validation in additional NSCLC and patient-derived models are required to establish their biological, therapeutic, or biomarker relevance.

title: Recent advances in scaffold-based KRASG12C inhibitors: SAR and biological evaluation insights.
authors: Bhattacharjee T, Kumar A, Singh TG et al.
abstract: Over the past decade, targeting Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) mutations has shifted from being considered an undruggable target to becoming a realistic therapeutic strategy with the development of KRASG12C inhibitors. This mutation replaces glycine with cysteine at codon 12, thereby reducing the GTPase activity by keeping the protein in its active GTP-bound state. This process activates downstream RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT signalling pathways and plays a crucial role in driving various cellular processes such as uncontrolled cell proliferation and survival in cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), colorectal cancer, and pancreatic cancer. In the present review, various KRASG12C inhibitors reported in the last five years are compiled according to their structural class, including quinazolines, pyrimidines, pyrido-pyrimidinones, and pyrrole-pyrimidines, along with PROTAC-based degraders. Among these, compound 12 exhibited strong antiproliferative activity against the KRASG12C-mutant H358 cell line with an IC50 value of 7.6 nM. The presence of a 2-fluorophenyl moiety made compound 12 the most active compound. Compound 18 was also identified as a highly effective PROTAC degrader with IC50 = 0.045 μM (45 nM) in MIA PaCa-2 cells. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis demonstrated that electrophilic warheads (acrylamide moieties) together with rigid heterocyclic scaffolds play a key role in enhancing potency and selectivity. Additionally, docking studies, biological evaluations, and in vivo findings are discussed to provide a clearer picture of the therapeutic potential of various KRASG12C inhibitors. Overall, the present review highlights the recent progress in the development of KRASG12C inhibitors for the treatment of cancer.

title: Divarasib Bests 1st-Generation KRASG12C Inhibitors.
abstract: Patients with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated non-small cell lung cancer who received the KRASG12C inhibitor divarasib were 42% less likely to experience disease recurrence or die than those who received the standard first-generation drugs sotorasib or adagrasib, an international phase III trial concluded. After a median follow-up of 14.3 months, the median progression-free survival was 9.8 months and 5.7 months, respectively.

title: Rethinking Postoperative Pain in the Era of Robotic Thoracic Surgery: A Surgeon's Perspective on Functional Recovery and Potential Oncologic Implications.
authors: Miyazaki T, Doi R, Matsumoto K
abstract: Persistent postoperative pain remains an incompletely resolved problem after minimally invasive thoracic surgery, despite expectations that robot-assisted thoracic surgery (RATS) would meaningfully outperform video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) in analgesia. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from randomized trials, cohort studies, and meta-analyses comparing acute and chronic pain outcomes between VATS and RATS, examines mechanisms and surgically modifiable risk factors underlying intercostal nerve injury and pain chronification, and evaluates the emerging concept of Return to Intended Oncologic Treatment (RIOT) as a perioperative endpoint linking pain control to oncologic recovery. Across randomized and propensity-matched comparisons, RATS has generally failed to demonstrate superior pain outcomes relative to VATS, and several studies suggest multiport robotic platforms may produce greater early pain than uniportal thoracoscopic approaches. Port number, operative time, and drainage duration emerge as modifiable surgical predictors of chronic pain, while inadequately controlled acute pain compromises functional recovery and is associated with delayed RIOT; direct evidence that pain independently influences RIOT or long-term survival remains limited, and this link should currently be regarded as a plausible, testable hypothesis rather than an established causal pathway. We conclude that, on the comparative evidence available to date, robotic instrumentation has not shown a consistent, clinically meaningful reduction in pain burden relative to VATS, and that pain management should be reframed as a shared surgical-anesthetic target relevant to oncologic recovery rather than a comfort-oriented endpoint alone. Emerging robotic platforms warrant evaluation against this expanded outcome set.

title: Effects of Immersive Virtual Reality and Relaxation Video on Symptom Severity, Distress, and Quality of Life in Lung Cancer Patients During Initial Chemotherapy Cycles: A Three-Arm Randomised Controlled Trial.
authors: Baysoy K, Izgu N, Ozdemir L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of immersive virtual reality (VR) and a theme-matched relaxation video (RV) on symptom severity, distress, and quality of life in lung cancer patients.
METHODS: In this open-label, three-arm, parallel-group randomised controlled trial, 315 patients were allocated (1:1:1) to the VR (n = 106), RV (n = 104), or control (CG; n = 105) group. During the first two chemotherapy cycles, the VR and RV groups were assigned two 20 min sessions of immersive nature-themed VR or theme-matched RV, while the CG received routine care alone. The primary outcome domain was symptom severity, assessed through within-session changes in ten individual Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale (ESAS) symptom scores; distress and quality of life were secondary outcomes. Data were analysed with linear mixed models, and between-group differences are reported with Bonferroni-adjusted 95% confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: Compared with the CG, the within-session improvement was greater for eight of the ten ESAS symptoms with VR and for five with RV; the largest differences were for well-being (VR 1.26 points, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.53; RV 0.76, 0.49 to 1.03), with smaller differences for tiredness, depression, and anxiety. Distress also decreased more with VR (1.04, 0.73 to 1.34) and RV (0.73, 0.42 to 1.03) than in the CG. VR improved more than RV for well-being (0.50, 0.22 to 0.77), tiredness (0.47, 0.16 to 0.79), and distress (0.31, 0.002 to 0.62). No intervention-specific effect emerged for nausea, lack of appetite, or quality of life.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with routine care, two sessions of VR or RV improved acute symptoms, mainly well-being, tiredness, depression, and anxiety, and reduced distress, with no intervention-specific effect on quality of life. The additional benefit of VR was small and, for the ESAS symptoms, below the minimal clinically important difference, so RV may be a practical and accessible option.
STUDY REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06863623.

title: Pan-Cancer Analysis Identifies LUC7L2 as a Prognostic Biomarker and Potential Functional Regulator of Prostate Cancer Progression.
authors: Yuan J, Zhan P, Liu J et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Cancer imposes a substantial global public health burden, and its initiation and progression involve complex dysregulation of gene expression regulatory networks. Methods: This study systematically evaluated the expression characteristics and prognostic value of LUC7L2 across pan-cancer types, with a particular focus on functional validation in prostate cancer. Using transcriptomic and proteomic data from multiple databases, immunohistochemical staining from the Human Protein Atlas, and single-cell transcriptomic datasets GSE137829 and GSE176031, we analyzed the expression patterns of LUC7L2 in various cancer types. Diagnostic and prognostic potential was assessed through ROC curve analysis, Cox regression, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics, while the functional role of LUC7L2 in prostate cancer tumorigenesis and progression was validated via in vitro assays. Results: Results showed that LUC7L2 was significantly upregulated in glioblastoma and prostate adenocarcinoma, and downregulated in lung adenocarcinoma and ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma, with diagnostic AUC values exceeding 0.7 across multiple tumor types. In prostate cancer, high LUC7L2 expression was significantly associated with a shortened progression-free interval (multivariate HR = 3.50, 95% CI 1.95-6.29, p < 0.001), with a meta-analysis of independent cohorts showing a consistent direction of effect (pooled HR = 1.14, 95% CI 0.90-1.44). Moreover, LUC7L2 exhibited strong correlations with microsatellite instability and tumor mutational burden across multiple cancer types. Single-cell analysis revealed that its expression was markedly higher in malignant cells than in immune or stromal cells. In vitro knockdown of LUC7L2 in prostate cancer cells led to significantly suppressed proliferation, increased apoptosis, S-phase cell cycle arrest, reduced invasion and migration capacities, enhanced senescence, and aggravated DNA damage. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that LUC7L2 is specifically overexpressed in malignant prostate cancer cells and independently associated with poor prognosis. It further validates its regulatory roles in proliferation, apoptosis, migration, and DNA damage repair, providing both theoretical and experimental evidence supporting LUC7L2 as a potential biomarker for prostate cancer.

title: Feasibility Is Not Benefit: Resectable, Irradiable, or Biologically Selected? A Critical Review of the Unresolved Local-Platform Question in Stage III/N2 NSCLC.
authors: Skarlos P, Georgakopoulos I, Kougioumtzopoulou A et al.
abstract: Stage III/N2 non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can often be treated with either surgery-based multimodality therapy or definitive chemoradiotherapy. Historical randomized trials showed that surgery improved local control without demonstrating an overall-survival benefit; neither platform demonstrated superiority, although none was designed to establish equivalence. In the immunotherapy era, both pathways have improved through separate evidence streams: perioperative trials compared immunotherapy with chemotherapy-based surgical controls, and PACIFIC compared durvalumab with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. Neither stream determines which complete modern pathway is better for a patient eligible for both, and cross-trial comparisons are confounded by differences in populations, randomization points, and endpoint definitions. This review distinguishes three questions that are often conflated: whether direct comparative evidence exists, how large any relative treatment effect may be, and whether sufficient clinical equipoise exists to justify randomization. Technical resectability, physiological operability, and irradiability define eligibility for a platform, not comparative benefit, and no current biomarker has been shown to modify the relative effect of the two platforms. Comparative uncertainty is most visible in multistation, bulky, or anatomically complex N2 disease, the most practicable starting point for randomization; superiority of either platform, however, has not been demonstrated at either end of the N2 spectrum. A staged randomized comparison of the complete modern pathways, with prespecified analyses of candidate treatment-effect modifiers, is proposed as a reasoned research strategy.

title: Liquid Biopsy-Guided Surgical Decision-Making in Oligometastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Toward Dynamic Risk Stratification in the Multidisciplinary Era.
authors: Magouliotis DE, Androutsopoulou V, Zotos PA et al.
abstract: Oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is defined anatomically by a threshold of five or fewer metastatic lesions across three or fewer organs. That definition is a proxy for a biological question it cannot answer: whether the metastatic process has been arrested at a stage where eradication of all detectable disease is curative. Randomized phase II trials of local consolidative therapy have shown median progression-free survival gains of 6.2 and 8.0 months and, in one trial, a median overall survival of 41.2 months vs. 17.0 months, yet median progression-free survival with local therapy did not exceed 14.2 months, and the phase II/III NRG-LU002 trial found no significant survival benefit from adding local therapy to maintenance therapy. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) measures molecular disease burden. In resectable NSCLC, preoperative ctDNA detection is associated with a higher risk of relapse; in oligometastatic disease, the baseline sample is instead the quantitative reference for response. ctDNA kinetics during induction therapy track systemic response before any operation, although no response threshold has been validated, and postoperative molecular residual disease anticipates radiological relapse by a median of approximately 5 months. This review synthesizes the evidence linking liquid biopsy to surgical decision-making and proposes, as a hypothesis for prospective testing, a dynamic risk stratification framework anchored on five plasma sampling points. We separate established prognostic evidence from untested hypotheses, address oncogene-driven and other oligometastatic states, and define the assay requirements, confounders and trial designs needed before ctDNA can select patients for or against thoracic resection.

title: Automated Opportunistic Bone Mineral Density Assessment at Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Incident Vertebral Fractures and Mortality.
authors: Löffler MT, Rühling S, Sollmann N et al.
abstract: Background Low-dose CT (LDCT) for lung cancer screening enables opportunistic volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) assessment, but its prognostic value is unclear. Purpose To evaluate fully automated LDCT-derived vBMD for predicting vertebral fractures and its association with mortality in individuals who heavily smoke. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis included 55-74-year-old individuals who heavily smoked (≥30 pack-years) from the CT arm of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), a multicenter randomized controlled trial of LDCT versus radiography (participants recruited August 2002 to April 2004). Automated SpineQ software (Bonescreen) was used to measure thoracic and lumbar vBMD (normal, ≥120 mg/cm3; low bone mass [osteopenia], 80 to <120 mg/cm3; osteoporosis, <80 mg/cm3) and vertebral fractures (Genant scale). The outcomes included 1- and 2-year incident vertebral fractures and 6-year mortality (active follow-up to 2009). Poisson and Cox models were adjusted for demographic variables, available comorbidities, and baseline vertebral fractures. Results The NLST included 26 722 participants in the CT arm, with 21 856 included in the present analysis (mean age, 61 years ± 5 [SD]; 12 854 male participants). The 2-year vertebral fracture incidence (n = 18 211 participants with 2-year LDCT) was 0.9% for those with normal bone mass, 2.0% for those with low bone mass (adjusted relative risk, 2.07 [95% CI: 1.70, 2.53]), and 5.9% for those with osteoporosis (adjusted relative risk, 3.40 [95% CI: 2.69, 4.30]). Mortality risk (n = 21 447 participants with completed follow-up [median, 6.65 years]) was associated with osteoporotic vBMD in men (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.24 [95% CI: 1.02, 1.50]). Conclusion Fully automated opportunistic assessment of spinal vBMD predicted vertebral fracture risk and was associated with mortality in men after adjustment. Individuals with osteoporotic vBMD who heavily smoked had a 2-year fracture incidence above the 5% treatment threshold according to current osteoporosis guidelines. Clinical trial registration no. title: Diagnostic Performance of Lung-RADS Categories in Patients With Histopathologically Evaluated Pulmonary Lesions: A Retrospective Study.
authors: Ertugrul M, Bozlar U, Guvenir D et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) categories for predicting malignancy in a selected cohort of patients with pulmonary lesions who underwent histopathological evaluation.
METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included patients with pulmonary lesions detected on computed tomography (CT) who underwent histopathological evaluation between January 2011 and February 2018, and their CT images were retrospectively classified according to Lung-RADS version 1.0. Patients were grouped by age and sex. Histopathologic examination was accepted as the gold standard test. Negative and positive results according to the Lung RADS guidelines and histopathological results were compared. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive, and negative predictive values were calculated as a result of this comparison.
RESULTS: A total of 161 patients were included, of whom 122 (75.8%) had malignant and 39 (24.2%) had benign histopathological findings. According to Lung-RADS, 151 patients (93.8%) were classified as positive and 10 (6.2%) as negative. Lung-RADS categories were significantly associated with histopathological outcomes ( P < 0.001), with malignancy rates increasing across categories. Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV were 99.2%, 23.1%, 80.1%, and 90.0%, respectively. Diagnostic performance was more favorable in older patients, particularly in the 55-80 age group (κ =0.407, P < 0.001), with similar findings observed in the 55-74 subgroup (κ =0.404, P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In this selected cohort of patients undergoing histopathological evaluation, Lung-RADS demonstrated high sensitivity but limited specificity for predicting malignant pulmonary lesions. We believe that prospective studies conducted using multicenter, standardized protocols involving larger patient groups will yield more accurate data.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Safety of Spatially Fractionated Radiotherapy for Malignant Tumors: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map.
authors: Shanbhag NM, Bin Sumaida A, Balaraj KS
abstract: Spatially fractionated radiotherapy (SFRT) concentrates high doses in selected tumor regions while delivering lower doses between them. This systematic review evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment delivery, and harms across SFRT techniques, with particular attention to comparative evidence. PubMed, Europe PMC, and ClinicalTrials.gov were last searched on September 19, 2026; CINAHL, CENTRAL, Scopus, and WHO ICTRP were last searched on August 7, 2026. The original searches and selection were conducted by the corresponding author, with substantive artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and human checks across review stages. The September extension introduced further AI-assisted source verification and analysis. Eligible reports described patients receiving intentional SFRT for malignant tumors. Results were grouped by clinical question and synthesized without meta-analysis. Appraisal used the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2), Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I), and design-matched Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools; selected comparative questions underwent Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) evaluation. The final corpus comprised 151 reports representing 137 investigations. Evidence was predominantly noncomparative, with heterogeneous treatments, outcome definitions, and follow-up. A prematurely terminated randomized trial documented one response among nine participants assigned to GRID plus standard radiotherapy, with one unknown outcome, and one among three assigned to standard radiotherapy. A nonrandomized study in bulky unresectable non-small-cell lung cancer reported responses in 19/20 PATHY participants versus 4/20 receiving conventional palliative radiotherapy, but prognosis-based allocation prevented causal interpretation. Certainty was very low for four defined comparative questions. Several cohorts reported early tumor shrinkage or symptom improvement, while prospective evidence also showed nonuniform pain changes, progression, and relapse after initial response. Severe complications included obstruction, late genitourinary injury, and fatal carotid hemorrhage. Differences in endpoints, treatment combinations, analysis units, missingness, and possible cohort overlap precluded a defensible pooled effect or unique participant total. Restrictions by source access, design, era, and overlap preserved descriptive evidence of activity and delivery but did not establish comparative superiority, durable benefit, or general safety. SFRT warrants indication-specific evaluation with defined patient-important outcomes, reproducible dosimetry, and complete toxicity follow-up. The protocol and subsequent robustness amendment were retrospective and unregistered. No specific funding was received.

title: From virtual reality to artificial intelligence-driven digital humans in perioperative lung cancer care: An updated scoping review and translational framework for pulmonary rehabilitation.
authors: Sun Y, Jin X, Wei X et al.
abstract: Digital pulmonary rehabilitation may improve access and continuity around lung cancer surgery, but virtual reality, scripted avatars, connected applications, and artificial intelligence (ai)-driven digital humans are frequently conflated. we conducted an updated scoping synthesis using a two-stage architecture: an inherited systematic review corpus searched through January 1, 2024, and a targeted PubMed/citation update from January 2, 2024, to August 31, 2026. Direct clinical studies were classified by operational Level 1-3 criteria. Risk of bias (RoB) was appraised with RoB 2 or ROBINS-I where feasible; implementation findings were mapped to Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, and Sustainability while separating reported barriers from framework-derived concerns. The direct map contained 19 completed reports and one protocol: 5 Level 1 fixed-display/immersive interventions, 14 Level 2 deterministic connected systems, no completed Level 3 digital human trials, and one Level 2/3 protocol candidate. In the inherited meta-analysis, digital rehabilitation was associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications (risk ratio: 0.45, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.30-0.66) and shorter chest tube duration (-1.53 days), whereas postoperative length of stay was not significantly reduced (-1.42 days, 95% CI: -3.45 to 0.62). Updated studies reported heterogeneous functional and workflow benefits, but no direct evidence validated Level 3 outcome superiority. Current evidence supports digitally delivered rehabilitation, not AI-driven digital humans. The proposed taxonomy converts this evidence gap into testable design requirements. Future trials should prioritize head-to-head comparisons, standardized outcomes, AI safety and external validation, geriatric accessibility, interoperability, health economics, and sustained real-world implementation.

title: Early and late CTCAE and patient-reported outcomes following breast radiotherapy in the REQUITE cohort.
authors: Bockstiegel T, Webb A, Aguado-Barrera ME et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The international REQUITE study and its follow-up studies (RADprecise/REQUITEplus) prospectively collected longitudinal data from patients undergoing radiotherapy for breast, prostate, or lung cancer. We present data from 2057 women with breast cancer, describing patient-reported outcomes and acute and late adverse effects.
METHODS: Patients were recruited between April 2014 and October 2016. Eligible patients received external-beam photon radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery, had no metastasis at inclusion, no other malignancy within the previous five years, and no prior breast irradiation. Blood samples were collected before radiotherapy for genotyping, molecular analysis, and biobanking. Standardised assessments included CTCAE v4, EORTC QLQ-C30 and BR23, MFI, GPAQ, and DICOM/DVH data. Follow-up continued annually for two years, extending to eight years at eligible sites.
RESULTS: Acute side effects peaked at end of radiotherapy, with erythema in 83-89% of patients. Grade ≥ 2 acute effects, including pain (11% versus 4.3%) and skin ulceration (4.8% versus 0.8%), were more frequent with normofractionation than hypofractionation. Grade ≥ 2 late effects affected between 0.6% and 16.8% of patients; skin induration was the most frequent late effect. Patient-reported outcome scores varied over time, with functional scale scores at two years similar to or higher than at baseline.
CONCLUSION: REQUITE provides real-world evidence of acute and late outcomes following normo- and hypofractionation, broadly consistent with published randomised trials. The dataset, combining clinical adverse effects, quality of life, dosimetric, and genetic data, is a resource for personalised radiotherapy research (www.requite.eu).

title: Neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy in resectable or borderline resectable non-small-cell lung cancer: the phase 2 MDT-BRIDGE trial.
authors: Reck M, Nadal E, Gay CM et al.
abstract: The phase 2 MDT-BRIDGE study is investigating perioperative durvalumab plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy (AEGEAN regimen) in resectable and borderline resectable non-small-cell lung cancer and chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by consolidation durvalumab (PACIFIC regimen) in patients who become unresectable after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy guided by multidisciplinary team assessments during the neoadjuvant period. The primary endpoint was the overall resection rate (descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing). Secondary endpoints included event-free survival, progression-free survival, pathological complete response rate (resectable patients cohort), circulating tumor DNA clearance between baseline and presurgery/pre-CRT and safety. Overall, 142 patients received neoadjuvant treatment; 64.8% and 35.2% were deemed resectable and borderline resectable at baseline, respectively. The overall resection rate (95% confidence interval) was 74.6% (66.7‒81.6) in a population that included more than one-third of patients with borderline resectable disease. R0 resection rate was 96.2% (90.6‒99.0) in those who underwent surgery. Overall, 131 (92.3%) patients had surgery (n = 106) or CRT (n = 25) after neoadjuvant treatment, and 117 (82.4%) patients received adjuvant (n = 94) or consolidation (n = 23) durvalumab. During adjuvant or consolidation durvalumab, maximum grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 7.4% of resected patients and 17.4% of CRT-treated patients, with 8.5% and 13.0% discontinuing treatment due to adverse events. This multidisciplinary team-guided approach was feasible and enabled delivery of curative-intent treatment (surgery or CRT), followed by durvalumab in most patients, and demonstrated encouraging preliminary efficacy with a manageable adjuvant or consolidation safety profile that was consistent with prior studies. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05925530 .

title: [Genomic alterations in thymic epithelial tumors: State of knowledge, and the interest of liquid biopsy].
authors: Chour A, Beljebbar N, Rivard L et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: In the absence of randomized phase III trial data, thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) are rare malignancies of the prevascular mediastinum managed according to the WHO histological and the Masaoka-Koga classifications.
STATE OF THE ART: Next-generation sequencing has revealed distinct mutational characteristics between thymomas, which are characterized by a low tumor mutational burden and a near-specific GTF2I mutation, and thymic carcinomas which are dominated by alterations in CDKN2A, TP53 and KIT. These findings open the way for novel therapeutic strategies, involving immune checkpoint inhibitors and multi-kinase inhibitors in advanced thymic carcinomas. Notwithstanding the potential of liquid biopsy as a non-invasive monitoring tool, specific biological obstacles in TETs currently limit its clinical applicability.
PERSPECTIVES: Recent confirmation of the interest of liquid biopsy in perioperative management of lung cancer raises the prospect of transferring this approach to TETs. The key challenge lies in identifying the biological marker most suited to the monitoring of longitudinal tumors.
CONCLUSIONS: Genomic profiling of TETs enhances (rather than supplants) the historical histological classification, and should progressively inform therapeutic stratification, particularly in cases of thymic carcinoma.

title: Experience of participating in a randomised controlled feasibility trial of surgery versus no surgery as part of multimodality treatment in stage III-N2 non-small cell lung cancer: PIONEER.
authors: Perry MB, Ward A, Baldwin DR et al.

title: Final Analysis of the Neotorch Study: Perioperative Toripalimab in Combination with Chemotherapy for Patients with Stage Ⅱ/Ⅲ Resectable Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Li ZM, Wu L, Wang WX et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interim analysis of the Neotorch study demonstrated significant benefit in event-free survival (EFS) and major pathological response (MPR) rate for perioperative toripalimab plus chemotherapy in patients with resectable Stage Ⅲ non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we report the final analysis results of the overall Stage Ⅱ and Ⅲ patients from this study.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Eligible patients with treatment-naïve resectable Stage II, or Stage IIIA, IIIB (N2) NSCLC, were randomized to receive toripalimab or placebo plus chemotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment (3 cycles), adjuvant treatment (1 cycle), and toripalimab or placebo monotherapy as maintenance treatment (up to 13 cycles). The primary endpoints of this study were EFS assessed by investigators and MPR evaluated by blinded independent pathologic review (BIPR) in Stage Ⅲ patients, as well as the overall Stage Ⅱ and Ⅲ patients.
RESULTS: A total of 501 patients in China were randomized (toripalimab arm: N=250, placebo arm: N=251). The baseline characteristics were generally balanced between the 2 arms. At the final analysis (median follow-up of 48.2 months), the investigator-assessed EFS was significantly improved in the toripalimab arm with stratified hazard ratio (HR) of 0.52 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.39, 0.68; stratified P <0.0001), and the median EFS in the toripalimab arm was not reached, while 20.2 months in the placebo arm. The inter-arm difference of MPR rate was statistically significant and clinically meaningful (47% vs 9%, P<0.0001). The OS prolongation was also statistically significant in the toripalimab arm (HR 0.66; 95% CI: 0.49, 0.89, P=0.0072), with median survival not reached in either arm. The safety profile was consistent with the interim analysis, with no new safety signals identified.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative toripalimab plus chemotherapy demonstrated durable and significant benefits on EFS, MPR, and OS in resectable Stage Ⅱ and Ⅲ NSCLC patients, with a manageable safety profile.

title: Extended follow-up of tarlatamab in patients with small-cell lung cancer after platinum-based chemotherapy in the randomized phase 3 DeLLphi-304 study.
authors: Rudin CM, Ahn MJ, Schuler M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In the DeLLphi-304 trial, at a median follow-up of <12 months, tarlatamab significantly improved overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and patient-reported outcomes (PROs), and demonstrated a favorable safety profile versus chemotherapy. We report efficacy and safety outcomes after extended follow-up in patients with small-cell lung cancer (SCLC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this phase 3, open-label trial, patients with SCLC whose disease had progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy were randomized (1:1) to receive either tarlatamab or chemotherapy (topotecan, lurbinectedin, or amrubicin) until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or death. The primary endpoint was OS. Secondary endpoints included investigator-assessed PFS, objective response, disease control, duration of response per RECIST v1.1, PROs, and safety.
RESULTS: As of data cutoff (18 February 2026), median OS was 13.6 and 8.4 months with tarlatamab and chemotherapy, respectively (median follow-up, 23.3 and 22.8 months). Median PFS was 4.2 and 3.2 months, respectively (median follow-up, 22.2 and 21.9 months). Kaplan-Meier estimated OS rates at 12/24 months were 55.9%/30.3% with tarlatamab versus 39.0%/14.9% with chemotherapy; corresponding PFS rates at 12/24 months were 20.6%/14.2% versus 5.9%/2.3%. Objective response rate was 35.4% with tarlatamab, including six confirmed complete responses versus 20.4% with chemotherapy; at data cutoff, ongoing responses were observed in 31.1% (28/90) versus 3.8% (2/52) of responders, respectively. Sustained disease control for ≥52 weeks was observed in 24.4% versus 4.3%.
