Treatment-related adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 3.2% versus 6.6%; grade ≥3 events decreased over time, with no serious TRAEs with onset ≥12 months. CRS and ICANS occurred early in treatment and were predominantly low grade.
CONCLUSIONS: With extended follow-up, tarlatamab continues to demonstrate sustained and durable clinical benefit and a favorable long-term tolerability profile versus chemotherapy, in patients with SCLC after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy, supporting its use as the standard of care in this setting.

title: Hypoxia-inducible CEA-targeted CAR T-cell therapy for relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Wei S, Guo J, Bai X et al.
abstract: Mitigating on-target off-tumor toxicity remains a central challenge for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for solid tumors. We developed a hypoxia-inducible CAR-T-cell product targeting carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) that restricts CAR activation to hypoxic tumor niches via oxygen-dependent expression control. In this first-in-human, phase I trial enrolling heavily pretreated patients with relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), a single infusion of the investigational product achieved an objective response rate of 47% and a disease control rate of 87%, with a manageable safety profile. Exploratory analyses showed that clinical outcomes were associated with baseline factors. Deep single-cell profiling indicated that the clinical response was associated with the expansion of hypoxia-adapted, tumor-reactive-like CD8+ T cells alongside coordinated functional maturation of natural killer (NK) cells. Collectively, these data provide clinical proof-of-concept for hypoxia-inducible CAR design and inform the rational development of strategies leveraging tumor microenvironmental features in solid tumor cellular immunotherapy.

title: Precision Microbiome Interventions in Oncology: From Predictive Biomarkers to Therapeutic Modulation of Immunotherapy Outcomes.
authors: Biazzo M, Soriani M, Micallef MP et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of multiple malignancies, yet durable clinical responses remain limited to a subset of patients. Accumulating evidence identifies the gut microbiome as a regulator of antitumour immunity that can influence treatment efficacy and toxicity through microbial metabolism, epithelial barrier integrity, inflammatory signalling, and host immune responses. This review critically evaluates the microbiome as both a predictive biomarker and therapeutic target in precision oncology. It moves beyond descriptive taxonomic associations by assessing emerging functional and mechanistic models that integrate microbial metabolites, ecological interactions, strain-level variation, and host-microbiome communication. Clinical and translational evidence from melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and urothelial carcinoma reveals marked differences in the reproducibility and clinical maturity of reported microbial signatures. Emerging microbiome-targeted strategies, including dietary modulation, faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), live biotherapeutic products (LBPs), and defined microbial consortia, may enhance ICI responsiveness, with responder-derived FMT providing important early clinical proof of concept. However, inter-individual variability, donor-recipient compatibility, microbial engraftment, the lack of standardised analytical approaches, and unresolved safety and regulatory requirements continue to limit clinical translation. Pending prospective validation, reasonable clinical practice is to avoid unnecessary microbiome-disrupting antibiotics, systematically document diet and concomitant medications, evaluate FMT and LBPs within regulated clinical trials, and interpret microbiome profiles alongside established tumour and host biomarkers rather than as stand-alone tests. Current evidence therefore supports a cautious shift towards functional microbiome-guided precision oncology, providing a foundation for personalised strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy outcomes.

title: An Overview of Cushing's Syndrome Caused by Ectopic Adrenocorticotropin Secretion.
authors: Ilias I, Maggio V, Ispas S et al.
abstract: Ectopic Cushing's syndrome (ECS) causes 10% to 20% of all cases of endogenous hypercortisolism. It is caused by the aberrant secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) due to the presence of an ectopic tumor. The latter is usually a neuroendocrine (NEN) tumor (mostly thoracic NENs such as bronchial NEN neoplasms, thymic NEN neoplasms, small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), or pancreatic NEN neoplasms). Clinical presentation is heterogeneous: an aggressive phenotype, typically driven by rapidly growing, poorly differentiated tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma, manifests with severe symptoms of acute onset, predominant myopathy, resistant arterial hypertension, hypokalemia, and severe hyperpigmentation, usually without the centripetal obesity typical of Cushing's syndrome; conversely, an indolent phenotype, more often related to well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms such as bronchial carcinoids, may present with the classic centripetal fat distribution, facial plethora, and purple striae also seen in Cushing's disease, making clinical distinction between the two difficult. The diagnosis of ECS can be cumbersome and time-consuming. Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, the most critical step is to distinguish patients with an ectopic source of ACTH from those with pituitary adenoma. Dynamic endocrine tests such as the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, CRH stimulation tests, desmopressin tests, and bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) can be helpful in the differential diagnosis. BIPSS is considered the gold standard for distinguishing a pituitary from a non-pituitary source of ACTH: the absence of a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient supports, but does not by itself localize or confirm, an ectopic source. Tumor localization is achieved by a multimodality imaging protocol, including initial high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scans, followed by functional imaging, mainly Gallium-68-labeled somatostatin receptor positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scans. However, in 10-20% of these patients, the tumors cannot be localized. The treatment of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism is two-fold: one is to immediately control hypercortisolism to prevent life-threatening complications (opportunistic infections and thromboembolism), and the second is to definitively treat the tumor. Medical treatment with steroidogenesis inhibitors, including metyrapone, ketoconazole, and osilodrostat, or surgical management (bilateral adrenalectomy) can be effective in immediately controlling hypercortisolism. Definitive surgical resection of the tumor is the hoped-for final treatment. The prognosis is variable, depending on the nature of the underlying neoplasm, ranging from excellent in patients with resected bronchial carcinoids to dismal in those with SCLC.

title: Adaptive Mitochondrial Specialization in Lung Adenocarcinoma: Redox Homeostasis, Hypoxia Adaptation, and Therapeutic Resistance.
authors: Castillejos-López M, Barrera-Elizalde U, Flores-Soto E et al.
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) exhibits metabolic flexibility that transcends the classical interpretation of the Warburg effect. This review proposes the concept of "adaptive mitochondrial specialization (AMS)", an integrative framework in which mitochondria undergo coordinated, context-dependent remodeling of bioenergetic metabolism, redox homeostasis, architecture and dynamics, proteostasis, mitochondrial genome maintenance and translation, and inter-organelle communication in response to hypoxia and other tumor-associated stressors. We examine how hypoxia can promote this adaptive state through HIF-dependent metabolic reprogramming together with intrinsic mitochondrial stress responses, including respiratory-chain remodeling, proteostatic regulation, and context-dependent control of reactive oxygen species (ROS). We further discuss mitochondrial genome and translational maintenance, fusion/fission dynamics, apoptotic susceptibility, and mitochondria-associated membrane (MAM) signaling as mechanisms through which mitochondrial function can be adjusted to environmental and therapeutic stress. Beyond tumor cells, we examine how mitochondrial quality-control alterations accompany systemic metabolic remodeling during cancer cachexia and how impaired mitophagy and intercellular mitochondrial transfer can influence antitumor T-cell function. These tumor-host manifestations are considered consequences or interacting mechanisms of cancer-associated mitochondrial remodeling rather than defining criteria of AMS. Finally, we discuss how context-dependent mitochondrial and redox dependencies may expose therapeutic vulnerabilities and provide a rationale for bioenergetic stratification in precision oncology.

title: Inspiratory muscle strength and skeletal muscle mass are associated with postoperative functional exercise capacity after lung cancer surgery: A retrospective cohort study.
authors: Rim H, Lee SH, Kim JS et al.
abstract: Although surgical resection is the cornerstone of curative treatment for early-stage lung cancer, patients often experience postoperative declines in physical fitness and skeletal muscle mass, resulting in reduced exercise capacity, which is associated with prognosis. This study aimed to identify clinical factors associated with postoperative functional exercise capacity, as measured by the incremental shuttle walk test, in patients undergoing lung cancer surgery. This retrospective study included 62 subjects (mean age, 67 ± 8.7 years; 24 women and 38 men) who underwent lung cancer surgery and completed a postoperative assessment at 3 months. Functional exercise capacity was assessed using the incremental shuttle walking distance (ISWD) as the primary outcome. Correlation and regression analyses were conducted to examine the associations between ISWD and concurrent measures of forced expiratory volume in 1 second, forced vital capacity, maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), maximal expiratory pressure, and skeletal muscle index (SMI). At 3 months postoperatively, ISWD was negatively correlated with age (r = -0.354, P = .005) and positively correlated with SMI (r = 0.253, P = .048) and predicted MIP (%; r = 0.293, P = .02), whereas other pulmonary function parameters were not significantly associated with ISWD. In regression models adjusted for 1-month ISWD, age, and sex, both predicted MIP (%; β = 0.290, P = .03; ΔR2 = 0.079) and SMI (β = 0.340, P = .03; ΔR2 = 0.075) were independently associated with 3-month ISWD. Subjects with low SMI demonstrated significantly lower 3-month ISWD than those with normal SMI (P = .02). Skeletal muscle mass and inspiratory muscle strength were associated with functional exercise capacity assessed using the incremental shuttle walk test at 3 months after lung cancer surgery. These findings suggest that assessment of muscle-related factors may improve the evaluation of postoperative functional recovery and help identify potential targets for rehabilitation.

title: Environmental Exposure to Carcinogens and Cancer Incidence in Kazakhstan: Opportunities for Cancer Prevention.
authors: Taioli E, Tuminello S, Henschke C et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kazakhstan is a large country in Central Asia with long history of uranium and asbestos mining and nuclear testing, whose health effects have not been fully analyzed.
OBJECTIVES: To study the geographical distribution of cancer rates in relation to toxic sites.
METHODS: We conducted an extensive review of publicly available datasets, administrative documents, and publications to assess past and active sources of exposure to carcinogens, and the geographic distribution of cancer incidence.
FINDINGS: Several past and ongoing sources of environmental exposures were identified. Cancer incidence is unevenly distributed, with the highest rates in the areas where nuclear testing was performed. The most frequently observed cancers are those of the lung, stomach, colorectum, and hematopoietic system. Among males, prostate cancer entered the list of the top cancers, while among females, breast, uterine, and cervical cancer were the most represented.
CONCLUSIONS: There are relatively small, densely populated areas that are heavily impacted by reactors, previous nuclear testing, uranium mines, chemical plants, and nuclear waste facilities. The geographic distribution of cancer rates reflects, in part, the location of the polluting sites, as well as personal exposure to behavioral risk factors, such as smoking and dietary habits. Aggressive preventive measures should be put in place for those cancers that are preventable through either screening or vaccination. Because of the many radon and uranium sites, lung cancer screening should be routinely offered to high-risk populations.

title: From motion to molecules: exercise-triggered large EVs suppress oncogenic signaling in lung adenocarcinoma cells - an in vitro pilot study.
authors: Adam Z, Garai K, Sebok-Tornai A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although regular physical activity is known to reduce cancer risk, the circulating molecular mechanisms responsible for these effects remain incompletely defined. Exercise alters the release and composition of extracellular vesicles (EVs), suggesting a role in systemic anti-tumor signaling. However, the contribution of large EVs (L-EVs) ─ a distinct and understudied EV subtype ─ to the regulation of lung adenocarcinoma cell behaviour has not been examined to date.
METHODS: L-EVs were isolated from platelet-free plasma of healthy, regularly exercising older adults with over 25 years of training history (aged 61 ± 2 years), collected at rest (Pre) and after (Post) an acute endurance exercise bout. EV fractions were characterized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM), nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), and antibody-based profiling. PC9 lung adenocarcinoma cells were incubated with plasma-derived L-EV-enriched fractions for 24 h. Cell viability and metabolic activity were evaluated using ATP-based luminescence and XTT assays following L-EV treatment. miRNA and gene expression changes were assessed using RT-qPCR with TaqMan arrays. Differentially expressed miRNAs (DEmiRs) and genes (DEGs) were analysed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) to evaluate regulatory networks and predict functional outcomes.
RESULTS: Exercise significantly increased plasma nanoparticle concentration (mean increase of 5.05 × 10⁷ ± 9.99 × 10⁶ particles/mL; p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.685). TEM and NTA confirmed successful isolation of L-EVs, with mode sizes of 136.1 ± 23.6 nm pre-exercise and 129.5 ± 17.7 nm post-exercise. In PC9 cells, both Pre- and Post-L-EVs reduced metabolic activity compared to control conditions, as demonstrated by ATP-based and XTT assays, indicating a functional impact on cell viability (p < 0.001). Transcriptomic analysis revealed distinct expression changes between conditions. Post-L-EVs downregulated oncogenic and immune evasion-associated genes (MAX, FASLG, and ELK1) while upregulating pro-apoptotic and cell cycle inhibitory genes (CASP9, FADD, and CDKN2B). Several DEmiRs, including miR-21-5p, miR-301b-3p, and miR-193a-3p, shifted in directions opposite to their known oncogenic patterns in NSCLC, suggesting a tumor-suppressive influence. IPA predicted enhanced apoptotic signaling and reduced metastatic potential following Post-L-EV treatment.
CONCLUSION: Exercise-conditioned plasma-derived enriched L-EVs modulate gene and miRNA expression in lung adenocarcinoma cells toward a tumor-suppressive profile. By attenuating oncogenic and immune-evasion signals while enhancing apoptotic and cell cycle-inhibitory pathways, Post-L-EVs offer preliminary mechanistic insight into the anti-cancer potential of physical activity. Their origin from older adults engaged in long-term exercise highlights the systemic benefits of sustained activity and the promise of L-EVs as biomarkers of exercise responsiveness.

title: Comparative Therapeutic Validation of a Microfluidic Metastasis Model: Cimetidine but Not Cilengitide Inhibits Physiological Tumor Cell Extravasation.
authors: Kühlbach C, Olschewski L, Baganz F et al.
abstract: Interactions between tumor cells and the endothelial lining of blood vessels under flow conditions are essential for successful metastasis. These interactions are mainly facilitated by adhesive proteins, like integrins or selectins and by proteases. While expression of specific integrins (αvβ3 and αvβ5) and selectins correlate with tumor progression in cancer and seem to mediate tumor cell adhesion, analysis of a therapeutic intervention in these processes is frequently limited to systems lacking physiological cell-cell interactions. In this study on the adhesion of different tumor cell types in monoculture and in coculture on endothelial cell layers was evaluated under different conditions, i.e., different static setups and under flow conditions in a microfluidic device and under treatment with the integrin inhibitor Cilengitide and the selectin inhibitor Cimetidine. This careful comparative experimental validation revealed that while Cilengitide inhibits H838-, HCT116- and U87-tumor cell adhesion in tumor cell monocultures in all assay set-ups its effect is abolished by the presence of endothelial cells. In contrast, Cimetidine, a Histamine 2 receptor antagonist and E-selectin inhibitor significantly reduced H838 lung carcinoma cell adhesion and trans-endothelial migration suggesting a significant role of E-selectin in tumor progressions and metastasis.

title: From Target Discovery to Spatial Delivery: A Translational Roadmap for Gene-Targeted Therapies in Glioma.
authors: Cheng H, Zhang Y, Zhu J et al.
abstract: Diffuse gliomas are increasingly defined by molecular alterations, yet the clinical translation of gene-targeted therapies remains constrained by a persistent mismatch between target biology and spatial pharmacology. In this review, we connect target discovery to clinical development by integrating spatial and longitudinal tumor biology with payload selection, delivery engineering, biomarker design, manufacturing, and mechanism-driven trials. Recent clinical practices in locoregional CAR-T cells, oncolytic and gene-delivery viruses, tumor-homing myeloid cell gene therapy, mutation- and neoantigen-directed vaccination, RNA nanomedicines, and emerging genome-editing strategies suggest that vehicle and route of administration dramatically change drug exposure, therapeutic index, immune activity, and resistance. We therefore propose the concept of "delivery-adjusted targetability," in which a candidate target is judged not only by biological dependency but also by clonality, longitudinal stability, normal-brain expression, anatomical distribution, modality compatibility, and achievable target engagement. We further argue that the clinically actionable unit in diffuse glioma is often a target-anatomical compartment pair rather than a molecular target considered in isolation. Moreover, we advocate target-payload-vehicle-route-biomarker co-design and a stage-gated evidence package. This framework provides a potential way to compare otherwise dissimilar platforms, distinguish target failure from delivery failure, and reject biologically attractive but spatially implausible programs earlier. Treating molecular dependency and spatial access as a single design problem can make precision neuro-oncology more experimentally falsifiable and clinically actionable.

title: Personalized Therapeutic Strategies in Glioblastoma: Bridging Molecular Markers and In Vivo Observations for Targeted Treatment.
authors: Fiallo Arroyo J, Leon-Rojas JE
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is still the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. It has a declining median survival rate and shows strong resistance to treatment. This resistance comes from significant differences within the tumor itself. The past failures of standard treatments have led to a shift in neuro-oncology. We now focus on molecular stratification based on genetic changes that can be targeted, instead of relying solely on histopathological classifications. This review looks at how important molecular drivers, like metabolic changes caused by IDH1/2 mutations, MGMT promoter methylation status, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling involving EGFR and EGFRvIII, and changes in epigenetics seen in H3 K27M, are creating new opportunities in immunotherapy, CAR-T cell therapy, precision radiation, and nanomedicine. We also discuss how preclinical validation through in vivo functional models, including patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) and syngeneic mouse lines, offers key insights into tumor evolution under treatment pressure, how drugs penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and the immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). However, despite the scientific backing for these therapies, recent Phase III clinical trial failures highlight a significant gap in translating these findings into effective treatments. This gap mainly results from random Darwinian clonal replacement and antigen escape. To address this issue, we explore the potential of liquid biopsies, such as cerebrospinal fluid and plasma, for real-time molecular tracking. These can help differentiate between true progression and pseudoprogression. Ultimately, we believe that closing the translational gap requires moving away from static clinical methods and adopting flexible, long-term trial designs. We also need to integrate multi-omic data with artificial intelligence (AI) to predict cellular changes and counteract resistance mechanisms before they lead to clinical recurrence.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle Delivery of CAR276 mRNA Enables Antigen-Specific Cytotoxicity in T Cells Against Glioblastoma Cells.
authors: Zahedipour F, Sadeghianfard S, Wisser S et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains the most aggressive and treatment-refractory primary brain tumor, with current therapeutic modalities providing minimal survival improvement. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapies succeeded in hematologic malignancies but are constrained in solid tumors by tumor heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironment, and delivery challenges. CD276 (B7-H3), a pan-cancer antigen overexpressed in gliomas and correlated with poor patient outcomes, represents a compelling immunotherapeutic target. Methods: Here, we developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for transient CAR mRNA delivery to T cells and evaluated its application for generating CD276 (B7-H3)-targeted CAR-T cells against GBM. An in-house-assembled T-mixer incorporating polyether ether ketone (PEEK) tubing was integrated with a dual-syringe-pump system for controlled LNP production. Results: LNPs formulated with clinically relevant ionizable lipids, SM-102 and DLin-MC3-DMA, demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and effective mRNA delivery. Cell-type-dependent expression kinetics were further characterized following LNP-mediated reporter mRNA delivery in K562, NK, NK92, and T cells, revealing differences in transgene expression across cell populations. LNP-mediated delivery of CD276 CAR mRNA enabled generation of CAR-expressing T cells that exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD276-positive LN229 GBM cells in vitro. Conclusions: Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptable LNP-based platform for non-viral CAR mRNA engineering of T cells and CD276-targeted cytotoxicity against GBM cells in vitro. The combination of transient CAR expression and LNP-mediated mRNA delivery provides a foundation for further optimization and evaluation in preclinical in vivo models.

title: Metabolic Rewiring of GPC3-Targeted CAR T Cells Expressing IL-15 and HER2-Targeted CAR T Cells via the ADA1-CD26 Axis Promotes Tumor Infiltration and Limits Systemic Toxicities.
authors: Hu Y, Song K, Wang R et al.
abstract: Background: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for solid tumors is limited by inadequate T-cell persistence and tumor infiltration, as well as treatment-associated cytokine release syndrome (CRS). To address these challenges, we developed a metabolically rewired CAR T-cell (MRCAR) platform by co-expressing adenosine deaminase 1 (ADA1) and CD26 in CAR T cells. Methods: MRCAR T cells were generated using either GPC3-targeted CARs for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) or HER2-targeted CARs for breast cancer. For HCC, we further evaluated constructs with and without enforced IL-15 expression to boost T-cell function. Results: In vitro, IL-15-expressing GPC3-MRCAR T cells exhibited enhanced proliferation, sustained effector function, reduced exhaustion, and superior cytotoxicity following repeated antigen stimulation compared with conventional CAR T cells. CD26 expression significantly enhanced CAR T-cell invasiveness in transwell assays and promoted tumor infiltration in vivo in both tumor models. ADA1 expression enhanced CAR T-cell persistence and was associated with increased frequencies of memory and stem-like T-cell populations in vivo. Notably, although IL15-GPC3-CAR T-cell treatment increased antitumor activity, it also caused high mortality and systemic inflammation in Huh7 tumor-bearing mice, whereas incorporation of ADA1 and CD26 into MRCAR T cells significantly improved survival and reduced serum levels of IL-6, IFN-γ, and TNF-α. Mechanistically, conventional IL-15-expressing GPC3-CAR T cells induced proinflammatory M1-like macrophage activation, whereas MRCAR T cells markedly suppressed this inflammatory response. Conclusions: Collectively, these results indicate that metabolic rewiring via ADA1 and CD26 enhances CAR T-cell expansion, tumor infiltration, persistence, and safety, supporting the MRCAR platform as a promising strategy to improve both efficacy and tolerability of CAR T-cell therapy for solid tumors.

title: Fast and Ultra-Fast mRNA-Engineered Anti-CA125/MUC16 CAR-T-Cells: An In Vitro Study.
authors: Aminulla K, Pilunov A, Maleeva A et al.
abstract: Background: Ovarian cancer treatment is frequently complicated by postoperative recurrence associated with metastatic dissemination and acquired chemotherapy resistance, highlighting the need for new therapeutic approaches. Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is a promising strategy for solid tumors because it enables transient CAR expression and may shorten the manufacturing process compared with lentiviral approaches. Given the potential relevance of rapid, transient CAR expression to locoregional or adjuvant applications, we evaluated an mRNA-based CAR-T cell approach targeting cancer antigen 125 (CA125) in vitro. Methods: CAR-T cells were generated from either activated or nonactivated ("resting") lymphocytes obtained from healthy donors using mRNA electroporation. Their activity against target tumor cells was assessed by impedance-based real-time cell analysis (RTCA) using the xCELLigence platform. Results: We compared two mRNA CAR-T cell manufacturing strategies: "fast" CAR-T cells generated using a 3-day activation-based workflow and "ultra-fast" CAR-T cells generated from nonactivated T cells and functionally evaluated within 24 h after electroporation. "Fast" CAR-T cells exhibited strong in vitro activity, including at an effector-to-target ratio of 1:4, representing a high target-cell burden. "Ultra-fast" CAR-T cells were also functional but showed lower activity, with an observable effect requiring an effector-to-target ratio of at least 2.5:1. Conclusions: These findings support the feasibility of rapid mRNA-engineered anti-CA125 CAR-T cell manufacturing using either activated or nonactivated T cells. The two approaches differ in functional activity and may therefore be suitable for different manufacturing workflows and intended applications.

title: The Antigen-Presentation Bottleneck in Pediatric Solid Tumors: Developmental Antigens, MHC-I Suppression, and Therapeutic Restoration of Tumor Immune Recognition.
authors: Alghoul WII, Qassim ZAM, Neyyappadath RJ et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pediatric solid tumors respond poorly to T-cell-directed immunotherapy despite expressing developmentally restricted, cancer-testis, fusion-derived, and lineage-associated antigens, suggesting that therapeutic failure may reflect defective conversion of intracellular antigen expression into surface peptide-major histocompatibility complex class I (pMHC-I) display. This review examines the antigen-presentation bottleneck as a framework for tumor immune invisibility and therapeutic resistance.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative mechanistic synthesis of pediatric and translational evidence on antigen repertoires, MHC-I and antigen-processing machinery dysfunction, mechanisms of presentation loss, therapeutic restoration, pMHC-directed immunotherapy, and MHC-independent bypass strategies.
RESULTS: Antigen expression does not reliably predict natural presentation. Presentation failure may result from HLA loss, coordinated transcriptional repression, developmental and epigenetic states, altered trafficking, SUMOylation, and autophagy-mediated MHC-I degradation. Potentially reversible defects can be targeted through cytokine signaling, NF-κB/IRF1/NLRC5 reactivation, epigenetic or lineage reprogramming, and inhibition of post-translational MHC-I loss; irreversible defects favor MHC-independent surface targeting.
CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric solid tumors may be antigen-invisible rather than antigen-poor. Therapeutic matching should assess antigen abundance, HLA integrity, antigen-processing competence, natural peptide presentation, quantitative pMHC density, and spatial and longitudinal heterogeneity, then restore presentation or deliberately bypass it. The framework distinguishes the presentation phenotype (quantitative pMHC insufficiency versus qualitative loss or functional absence of a required HLA/APM element) from the underlying mechanism (soft/potentially reversible versus hard/structural) because these dimensions have different biomarker and therapeutic implications.

title: Immunotherapy in the Treatment of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Review of Current Evidence, Emerging Strategies and Future Directions.
authors: Smith-Salzberg B, Resende Salgado L, Yu C et al.
abstract: Introduction: Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) are among the most common cancers worldwide and continue to carry substantial morbidity and mortality despite advances in surgery, radiation therapy (RT), and systemic therapy. Treatment varies according to disease stage, clinical setting, and prior therapy. The immunologically active tumor microenvironment of HNSCC and expression of immune-regulatory pathways have made immunotherapy an important area of therapeutic development. Methods: This is a narrative review of the established and emerging immunotherapeutic strategies for HNSCC, their clinical applications, mechanisms of resistance, and future directions. We used relevant search terms in PubMed to examine the available literature. Discussion and Conclusions: We discuss several immunotherapeutic agents, including PD-1, PD-L1 and CTLA-4 inhibitors, as well as emerging immune checkpoint targets such as LAG-3, TIGIT, TIM-3 and VISTA. We also consider the importance of HPV status in prognosis and treatment response. The role of immunotherapy is considered across disease stages and treatment settings, with particular emphasis on recurrent or metastatic HNSCC and locally advanced HNSCC in the perioperative setting, for which PD-1 inhibitors have demonstrated the clearest clinical benefit and have become an important component of standard therapy. We also review the expanding role of neoadjuvant and adjuvant immunotherapy, as well as combinations with RT, for which efficacy remains under investigation or has been inconsistent across clinical trials. In addition, we examine mechanisms of primary and acquired resistance related to tumor biology and molecular mutations. Finally, we highlight emerging therapeutic approaches, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, therapeutic cancer vaccines, and combinations of immunotherapy with proton beam therapy. Together, these developments illustrate the rapidly expanding role of immunotherapy across HNSCC treatment and identify areas in which further investigation may expand therapeutic options and improve outcomes.

title: Reprogramming the Melanoma Tumor Microenvironment: From Cellular Crosstalk to Cellular Immunotherapy.
authors: Jumaniyazova E, Gantsova E, Kazarian G et al.
abstract: Melanoma is the most aggressive and rapidly metastasizing malignant neoplasm of the skin and mucous membranes, arising from melanocytes of neuroectodermal origin. Despite substantial advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy, a significant proportion of patients develop primary or acquired resistance, which is largely attributable to the complex interactions between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the cellular and molecular components of the melanoma TME and their contribution to immunosuppression, tumor progression, and therapeutic resistance. The role of keratinocytes as the primary niche-forming cells in the epidermis is examined, including their reprogramming during melanomagenesis and their involvement in drug resistance. Particular attention is given to cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which orchestrate stromal remodeling, promote immune exclusion, and limit the efficacy of immunotherapy. The phenotypic and functional heterogeneity of innate and adaptive immune cells-macrophages, granulocytes, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, T and B lymphocytes-is discussed in the context of their dual role in antitumor immunity and immune escape. A detailed analysis of immune editing mechanisms, including defective antigen recognition, resistance to apoptosis, and the establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment, is provided. The review further summarizes the current landscape of cellular immunotherapy for melanoma. Clinically established approaches, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and CAR-T cells, are discussed with reference to completed phase II-III clinical trials, whereas emerging strategies such as CAR-macrophages and dendritic cell vaccines are presented as largely preclinical or early-phase investigational platforms. It is concluded that the melanoma TME functions as a unified immunosuppressive network rather than a collection of individual cell populations. Based on currently available comparative clinical evidence, reprogramming this network through the combination of cellular platforms with immune checkpoint inhibitors, stromal modulators, and macrophage-repolarizing agents, supported by personalized assessment of TME composition, represents a rational and actively investigated therapeutic direction.

title: Low-affinity anti-HER2-CAR T cells efficiently eradicate HER2+ and HER2low cancer cells with reduced toxicity on healthy tissue.
authors: Knoedler L, Herfeld K, Scherer JN et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is considered a therapeutic breakthrough in hematological malignancies. However, its translation to metastasized solid tumors remains limited by the paucity of "druggable" targets and the limited therapeutic potency of the cell therapeutics in solid cancers. Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), a promising target for treatment of metastasized solid cancers, is amplified in around 3% (HER2+ cancer) and overexpressed without amplification in ∼40% (HER2low cancer) of all carcinomas, yet the physiological expression of HER2 on healthy tissues poses the risk of on-target off-tumor effects. To address this, we utilized low-affinity (LA) Anti-HER2-CAR T cells. These CAR T cells exhibited efficient lysis of HER2+ SKOV3 ovarian cancer cells even at low effector-to-target ratios. Following stimulation through cancer cells, LA Anti-HER2-CAR T cells showed rapid proliferation and elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines markers. Low numbers of CAR T cells were sufficient to induce durable complete remissions of systemically seeded ovarian cancer in NOD-Prkdc scid -IL2rg Tm1 /Rj mice. LA Anti-HER2 CAR T cells also exhibited tumor regression and lasting tumor control in a subcutaneous in vivo model of HER2low LS174T cells. Additionally, the LA and high-affinity (HA) CAR T cells could effectively combat HER2low human colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines and primary CRC organoids, while LA Anti-HER2-CAR T cells showed a trend-wise reduced lysis of healthy colon organoids. Our results suggest that LA Anti-HER2-CAR T cells provide a novel treatment option for HER2-overexpressing advanced systemic tumors. Importantly, they effectively distinguished between healthy colon tissue and HER2low cancer, broadening the scope of HER2-directed CAR T cells to this frequent cancer subset.

title: From failure to fate: Pressure-driven exhaustion in solid-tumor CAR T-cell therapy.
authors: Wang P, Zhou Y, Wang Y et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has achieved remarkable and durable responses in hematologic malignancies, but its efficacy in solid tumors remains limited and frequently transient. In this Review, we propose that interacting tumor barriers divert persistently engaged CAR-T cells toward dysfunctional and exhausted states. Defective trafficking, antigen heterogeneity, incomplete tumor clearance, metabolic deprivation, stromal exclusion, immunosuppressive cellular networks, inhibitory cytokines, chronic CAR signaling, and manufacturing-imprinted stress collectively shape the stimulation history and functional trajectory of CAR T-cells. Mechanistically, these pressures converge on NFAT-AP-1 imbalance, TOX/TOX2 and NR4A activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and exhaustion-associated epigenetic remodeling. This process creates a clinically relevant continuum between TCF1-positive progenitor-exhausted cells that retain self-renewal and checkpoint-responsive proliferative potential, and terminally exhausted cells with limited regenerative capacity. Building on this failure-pressure-fate model, we propose a mechanism-informed therapy framework that relates dominant failure mechanisms and residual CAR T-cell plasticity to potential intervention priorities. This approach may help match combination strategies to the dominant tumor pressure and CAR T-cell state, including stromal remodeling, metabolic engineering, cytokine armoring, checkpoint modulation, epigenetic intervention, and remanufacturing. Overall, this Review provides a fate-based framework for designing next-generation CAR T-cell therapies capable of achieving durable control in solid tumors.

title: Gene therapy as an upcoming technique in the treatment of cancer: A cellular solution to a cellular problem.
authors: Bedada AT, Genet S
abstract: Cancer remains a formidable global health challenge, representing the second leading cause of mortality worldwide. In 2023, there were approximately 18.5 million new cancer cases and over 10 million deaths globally, with projections estimating 30.5 million new cases and 18.6 million deaths annually by 2050. In the US, an estimated 2,114,850 new cases and 626,140 deaths are projected for 2026. Cancer arises from accumulated genetic and epigenetic alterations that progressively transform normal cells into malignant counterparts, with mutations in proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair machinery as fundamental drivers of carcinogenesis. Gene therapy has emerged as a therapeutic modality that addresses cancer at its genetic core. This review examines the genetic basis of cancer pathogenesis and analyzes contemporary gene delivery platforms viral vectors, bacterial vectors (bactofection), physical methods (microinjection, electroporation, hydroporation, and gene gun), and chemical approaches (lipofection, polymer based systems, and nanoparticles)alongside their advantages, limitations, and clinical applications. Particular emphasis is placed on suicide gene therapy and immunomodulatory approaches, with focused examination of chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy as the most clinically advanced gene therapy strategy to date. Recent advances, including expanded regulatory designations for CAR-T therapies targeting solid tumors and next-generation vector platforms, underscore the field's rapid evolution. Despite persistent challenges safety concerns, high costs, and limited efficacy in solid tumors, gene therapy represents a transformative approach that may ultimately achieve durable remissions. We conclude by discussing future directions, including next-generation delivery systems, genome editing technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 base and prime editing, and strategies to improve accessibility and affordability.

title: An Australian Narrative Review of Adoptive Cellular Therapies in Malignancy: Expanding Indications, Referral Pathways and Safety Beyond Specialist Centres.
authors: Childs S, Ma D, Rodrigues A et al.
abstract: Adoptive cellular therapies (ACT), including tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL), T-cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies, represent an evolving class of immunotherapies with established efficacy in selected haematological malignancies and emerging applications in solid tumours. Additional platforms under investigation include virus-specific T cells, tumour-associated antigen-specific T cells, natural killer (NK) cell therapies and dendritic cell-based therapies. The therapeutic scope of ACT is expanding beyond oncology into autoimmune and fibrotic diseases, infectious diseases and inherited metabolic and immune disorders, highlighting the broad potential of cellular immunotherapy platforms. In solid tumours, efficacy remains limited by tumour antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive tumour micro-environment and impaired immune cell trafficking and persistence. These barriers are driving development of next-generation cellular products and combination strategies. Characteristic immune-mediated toxicities, particularly cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), remain important considerations. Although potentially severe, these toxicities are generally manageable with early recognition, multidisciplinary care and prompt specialist intervention. As ACT indications expand in Australia, clinician familiarity with indications, mechanisms of action and toxicity profiles is essential to support informed patient discussions, appropriate patient selection, timely referral and prompt toxicity recognition and management. Non-oncology specialists have an important role in shared care, including patient identification, referral coordination, monitoring for delayed or late toxicities and provision of ongoing survivorship and supportive care. Achieving equitable national access to ACT will require streamlined health technology assessment processes, coordinated reimbursement and delivery funding models and structured referral networks with cross-institutional collaboration to support the specialised infrastructure required for their delivery.

title: Effectiveness of NKG2D CAR-NK92 cells in targeting solid tumors: novel dynamic cytotoxicity analysis via real-time cell analysis.
authors: Wang X, Gong F, Li Y et al.
abstract: Lung, colorectal, and liver cancers are among the most prevalent and lethal solid tumors globally. However, traditional therapeutic modalities and even current immunotherapeutic strategies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy have failed to deliver durable clinical benefits. This limitation is primarily attributed to the challenges posed by tumor heterogeneity, off-target toxicity, and, critically, to the inadequate assessment of the dynamic anti-tumor efficacy of these treatments. A major bottleneck in the preclinical evaluation of CAR-based immunotherapies for solid tumors is the overreliance on static endpoint cytotoxicity assays, including lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release and chromium-51 (51Cr) release assays. These conventional methods merely quantify the final extent of tumor cell lysis and are unable to capture critical kinetic parameters-such as response latency, cytotoxicity rate, and the capacity for complete tumor elimination in vitro-all of which are pivotal for predicting clinical applicability. To address this gap, we employed real-time cell analysis (RTCA), a label-free and continuous monitoring technology, to systematically evaluate the anti-tumor potency of NKG2D CAR-engineered NK92 cells against lung (H1299), colorectal (HCT116), and liver (Hep3B) cancer cell lines. RTCA's unique capability to track tumor cell viability at 15-min intervals revealed that NKG2D CAR-engineered NK92 cells initiated cytotoxicity immediately without a lag phase, exhibited steeper cytotoxicity slopes, and achieved complete target cell eradication at an effector-to-target (E:T) ratio of 5:1-dynamic insights that remained undetectable with static assays. Notably, using this advanced cell killing detection method, we found that NKG2D CAR-engineered natural killer (NK) cells displayed cytotoxicity kinetics comparable to those of five times the number of unmodified NK cells against H1299, HCT116 and Hep3B cell lines. At E:T ratios of 5:1, the engineered cells also secreted significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ and TNF-α) compared to unmodified NK92 cells. This confirmed robust immune activation that coincided with real-time tumor killing. These findings not only demonstrate that NKG2D CAR-engineered NK92 cells represent a promising immunotherapeutic candidate for solid tumors, but also highlight RTCA as a useful and informative platform for monitoring cytotoxicity kinetics in real time and advancing the translational development of solid tumor immunotherapies.

title: Retraction Note: Engineered outer membrane vesicles enhance solid tumour CAR-T cell therapy.
authors: Li X, Li X, Shi J et al.

title: GD2IL18CART Combined With Bevacizumab for Relapsed and Refractory GD2-positive Solid Tumors
summary:
This study will test a CAR T-cell treatment combined with bevacizumab in children and young adults with relapsed or refractory neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, or osteosarcoma.

The CAR T-cell treatment, called GD2IL18CART, is made from a patient's own T cells. The T cells are genetically modified to recognize GD2, a molecule found on the surface of these cancers, and to release the immune-stimulating protein interleukin-18 (IL-18) when they encounter tumor cells. Bevacizumab is an antibody that blocks vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a protein that affects tumor blood vessels and may make it difficult for immune cells to enter tumors. Combining bevacizumab with GD2IL18CART may therefore help more CAR T cells reach the tumor and improve their antitumor activity.

The main goals of this study are to determine whether the combination can be given safely, identify a recommended dose of GD2IL18CART for use with bevacizumab, and look for early evidence of antitumor activity. The study will also examine blood and tumor samples to better understand how the treatment affects CAR T cells and the tumor environment.

title: Testing the Addition of an Anti-cancer Drug, Copanlisib, to the Usual Immunotherapy (Nivolumab With or Without Ipilimumab) in Patients With Advanced Solid Cancers That Have Changes in the Following Genes: PIK3CA and PTEN
summary: This phase I/II trial studies the side effects and best dose of copanlisib when given together with nivolumab and ipilimumab and to see how well they work in treating patients with solid cancers that may have spread from where it first started to nearby tissue, lymph nodes, or distant parts of the body (advanced) and have changes in PIK3CA and PTEN genes. Copanlisib may stop the growth of tumor cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth. Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies, such as nivolumab and ipilimumab, may help the body's immune system attack the cancer, and may interfere with the ability of tumor cells to grow and spread. The addition of copanlisib to usual immunotherapy may work better in treating patients with solid cancers compared to usual immunotherapy alone.

title: Cancer cells acquire cysteine directly from a reduced tumor microenvironment
summary: The metabolic environment of a tumor is shaped by the nutrients available in its interstitial fluid, yet the redox composition of that fluid is poorly defined. Measuring sulfur metabolites in the interstitial fluid of tumors, matched healthy organs, and serum across three mouse models of cancer, we find that the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a chemically reduced compartment in which free cysteine predominates over its oxidized form, cystine. This is especially pronounced in the lung TME, where cystine is nearly absent. We further show that lung cancer cells take up cysteine and cystine with comparable efficiency and proliferate on cysteine alone, and that the abundant glutathione in the TME helps keep cysteine reduced through disulfide exchange. In a medium formulated to match the sulfur composition of the lung tumor interstitial fluid, cells become independent of cystine import through xCT. Cells cultured in this medium were resistant to glutaminase inhibitors, oxidants and ferroptosis inducers, and better maintained NADPH levels under oxidative challenge. These findings suggest that standard culture conditions overestimate the dependence of cancer cells on cystine uptake and their vulnerability to oxidative stress-targeting therapies.

title: Quantifying epigenetic reprogramming and cellular plasticity in preneoplastic lesions reveals dedifferentiation as a key precancer hallmark
summary: Epigenetic reprogramming and plasticity are two cancer hallmarks that increase the risk of carcinogenic transformation, yet quantifying these properties remains a fundamental challenge. Here we develop and validate a general pan-tissue computational framework called PLASTIC for quantifying cellular plasticity and epigenetic reprogramming from single-cell RNA-seq data. PLASTIC allows construction of Waddington-like landscapes allowing identification of high cancer risk states. When applied to a pan-preneoplastic tissue setting, PLASTIC reveals how the level of epigenetic reprogramming of precancerous cells correlates with cellular plasticity and cancer-risk, and that the high cancer risk state is characterized by increased dedifferentiation, even when compared to its fetal cell counterpart. Furthermore, PLASTIC predicts the emergence of metaplasia in normal lung cells from smokers, identifying a high cancer risk signature that we validate in independent data. In summary, PLASTIC can help quantify cellular plasticity and dedifferentiation of single cells in any tissue-type, opening up new strategies for cancer risk prediction and prevention.

title: Targeting alpha-ketoglutarate starvation within the tumor-immune microenvironment rescues T cell effector function in cancer immunotherapy
summary: Given its status as the leading cause of global cancer mortality, there is a critical need to enhance immunotherapy strategies for lung cancer to overcome widespread resistance to current treatments. Immunotherapy recruits the patient's immune system to attack and destroy cancer cells. While highly effective in a subset of patients, chronic exposure of immune cells to cancer cells leads to a progressive loss of effector T cell function and progression of T cell exhaustion; now considered two well-established hallmarks of immunotherapy resistance. The tumor-immune microenvironment (TIME)-driven differentiation into the exhausted T cell phenotype is marked by a loss of metabolic plasticity and epigenome-wide changes in distribution of repressive histone marks such as histone H3 subunit methylation at lysine 27 (H3K27me3). Here, we studied how these processes are connected to metabolite availability within the TIME. In vitro, chronic antigen stimulation and hypoxia led to rapid loss of effector function, associated with a suppression of alpha-ketoglutarate (aKG) intracellular concentrations in T cells. Supplementation of cell-permeable aKG led to a rescue of effector cytokine production and to improved cytotoxic capacity despite chronic antigen stimulation and hypoxia. Increased intracellular aKG levels restored the activity of H3K27 demethylases UTX and JMJD3, consistent with epigenome-wide decreased H3K27me3. In vivo, dietary supplementation with commercially available calcium-aKG (Ca-aKG) supplements led to an elevation of serum and intratumoral aKG levels associated with a significant increase of immunotherapy effectiveness in mouse models of NSCLC. Clinical samples from patients with NSCLC contained significantly decreased serum aKG levels in older NSCLC patients (>65 years of age). Analysis identified a novel association between serum aKG levels and poor immunotherapy response. Thus, our work demonstrates that intratumoral metabolite starvation can be therapeutic

title: Clinicopathological and prognostic analysis of anaplastic lymphoma kinase-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Kayawake H, Mineura K, Sakanoue I et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 2‒7% of NSCLC cases and is prone to lymph node and distant metastases. We analyzed the clinicopathologic features and prognosis of patients with ALK-rearranged NSCLC who underwent surgery.
METHODS: This study included 30 patients who underwent surgery for ALK-rearranged NSCLC between January 2017 and September 2025, representing ~ 1.6% of all primary lung cancer surgeries performed during the same period.
RESULTS: The median age was 68 years, 19 patients were male, and 14 (46.7%) had a smoking history. Clinical stages were I (n = 22), II (n = 1), and III (n = 7). Lobectomy was the most common surgical procedure (n = 19), followed by partial resection (n = 6) and segmentectomy (n = 5). Complete resection was achieved in 26 (86.7%) patients. Pathological upstaging occurred in 11 (36.7%) patients. Postoperative recurrence occurred in 10 patients after complete resection, with a median recurrence-free interval of 554.5 days; eight patients received an ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitor (ALK-TKI). Among five patients with clinical stage III NSCLC receiving induction chemoradiotherapy, four underwent complete resection, but all experienced postoperative recurrence. The 5-year overall survival rate of the entire cohort was 89.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 64.1‒97.3%), while the 5-year recurrence-free survival rate after complete resection was 51.2% (95% CI 27.4‒70.7%).
CONCLUSIONS: Given the high recurrence rates associated with conventional perioperative treatment and occasional unexpected upstaging, a treatment strategy centered on surgical resection and ALK-TKIs may be important for ALK-rearranged NSCLC.

title: Uncovering KRAS-mutant allele-specific biology and vulnerabilities in non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: d'Arienzo PD, McDaid WJ, Tinsley KL et al.
abstract: KRAS (Kirsten-Ras) mutations are the most commonly occurring oncogenic drivers in non-small cell lung cancer. Despite the discovery of KRAS inhibitors representing a translational breakthrough for KRAS-driven cancers, resistance remains a major clinical challenge. We believe that to circumvent resistance, an in-depth understanding of the biological differences and therapeutic vulnerabilities specific to KRAS mutations is critical to inform rational combination partners with either mutant-selective or broad-spectrum (K)RAS inhibitors. The present review draws upon insights from both preclinical and clinical studies exploring KRAS-mutant allele-specific behaviours and therapeutic vulnerabilities. We will also highlight studies in which targeting of these vulnerabilities was combined with (K)RAS inhibitors, offering contextual examples of KRAS-mutant allele-tailored therapeutic strategies.

title: Efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitor plus bevacizumab-based chemotherapy in advanced or recurrent KRAS-mutant non-squamous NSCLC: the SPIRAL-STONE study.
authors: Ishida M, Yamada T, Kamada R et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS)-mutant lung cancer is associated with a poor prognosis, underscoring the need for effective pharmacological treatments. An exploratory subgroup analysis of IMpower150 suggested potential clinical benefit of the atezolizumab-containing regimen in KRAS-mutant non-squamous NSCLC, although prospective data remain limited. We prospectively evaluated its efficacy and safety and performed exploratory biomarker analyses.
METHODS: The study cohort comprised patients with advanced or recurrent KRAS-mutant non-squamous NSCLC scheduled to receive ICI plus bevacizumab-based chemotherapy at 10 Japanese institutions between January 2023 and December 2024. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included disease control rate (DCR), objective response rate (ORR), overall survival (OS), and safety. Associations between baseline serum levels of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-A and VEGF-D and treatment outcomes were explored in patients with available pretreatment samples.
RESULTS: Of 22 enrolled patients, 21 received treatment and were analyzed for efficacy and safety; 17 were analyzed for serum biomarkers. All patients received atezolizumab, bevacizumab, carboplatin, and paclitaxel. The median PFS and OS were 6.0 and 17.1 months, respectively. Among 19 patients with measurable disease, the ORR was 42.1%, and the DCR was 68.4%. Grade ≥3 hematologic and non-hematologic adverse events occurred in 33.3% and 47.6% of patients, respectively. Baseline serum VEGF-A and VEGF-D levels were not significantly associated with the treatment outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: ICI plus bevacizumab-based chemotherapy showed an ORR of 42.1%, a median PFS of 6.0 months, and a median OS of 17.1 months in patients with KRAS-mutant non-squamous NSCLC. Given the small sample size and single-arm design, these findings should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Pretreatment serum VEGF-A and VEGF-D levels were not significantly associated with clinical outcomes, although limited statistical power precludes definitive conclusions. Larger comparative studies with comprehensive molecular profiling are warranted.

title: Clinical and Demographic Characteristics of Patients with Pulmonary Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma: A Single-Center Experience.
authors: Özufacık Bölükbaşı Y, Aytekin A
abstract: Background and Objectives: Pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (pLCNEC) is a rare malignancy, accounting for approximately 2-3.5% of surgically resected primary lung cancers. Given its rarity, pLCNEC has been less extensively studied than other, more common lung cancer subtypes. In this study, we evaluated and compared the diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to pLCNEC. Materials and Methods: Patients with pLCNEC were evaluated with respect to age, sex, smoking history, primary tumor site, surgical history, tumor stage, histological subtype, metastatic sites at initial diagnosis and during follow-up, first- and second-line chemotherapy regimens, and disease survival parameters. Results: A total of 55 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. The median age at diagnosis was 63 years, the mean smoking exposure was 45.8 pack-years, and the median overall survival (mOS) for the entire cohort was 9 months (95% CI, 7-11). At presentation, 12.7% of the patients had stage I-II, 29.1% had stage III, and 58.2% had stage IV disease. Primary tumors were located peripherally in 85.5% of cases and centrally in 14.5%. A platinum plus etoposide regimen-standard for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC)-was the most commonly administered first-line chemotherapy (n = 40). Among all patients, 19 had undergone upfront surgical resection, whereas 36 had not. In univariate analysis, patients with a history of surgery (n = 19) had a significantly longer mOS than those without surgery (n = 36): 16 months (95% CI, 8-NR) versus 7 months (95% CI, 3-9), respectively (p = 0.003). On multivariate analysis, stage IV disease, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and advanced age were independently associated with poorer survival. In multivariable analyses, surgery showed a borderline association with survival that did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.052). Furthermore, median survival was significantly longer in patients with T1 stage disease compared with those with T3 and T4 stage, and in those with T3 compared with T4 stage (p = 0.045). Conclusions: Overall, early-stage diagnosis and surgical intervention may be associated with favorable clinical outcomes and a survival benefit.

title: Dynamic Monitoring of CTCs and EVs to Predict Chemoimmunotherapy Efficacy in Lung Cancer.
authors: Zhao C, Cheng L, Yu J et al.
abstract: Background: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs), programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) positive CTCs (PD-L1+CTCs) and extracellular vesicles (EVs) are important biomarkers for predicting treatment efficacy. This study comprehensively investigated the factors used to forecast chemoimmunotherapy efficacy in advanced lung cancer. Methods: The CellSearch system, EVAnalyzer plugin and single-cell whole-exome sequencing (WES) were used to analyze these factors. Results: It was found that CTCs were highly detectable in advanced lung cancer. The median number of baseline CTCs was significantly lower in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) than small cell lung cancer (SCLC) (3 vs. 38, p < 0.0001), as were PD-L1+CTCs (1 vs. 5, p = 0.0014). PD-L1+CTCs decreasing after two treatment circles was associated with superior ORR. Baseline median EV counts were elevated in NSCLC compared with SCLC (11,700 vs 1371, p = 0.017). Patients exhibiting divergent dynamic trends between EVs and CTC/PD-L1+CTCs demonstrated better treatment response. The combination of CTCs, PD-L1+CTCs and EVs improved predictive efficacy for both NSCLC and SCLC. CTC sequencing identified multiple pathogenic somatic variants, which might affect immunotherapy efficacy. Conclusions: Serial dynamic monitoring of CTCs, PD-L1+CTCs and EVs, as well as CTC sequencing, enables the early prediction of chemoimmunotherapy response and the discovery of mechanisms that affect immunotherapy efficacy in advanced lung cancer.

title: Sequencing of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy and Chemotherapy in Stage I Small Cell Lung Cancer: Practice Patterns and Outcomes.
authors: Ziaks TJ, Oh P, Hicks D et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: We evaluated practice patterns and survival outcomes associated with the sequencing of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and chemotherapy in patients with clinical stage I small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in the United States.
METHODS AND MATERIALS: Using a large national database, we identified patients with clinical stage I (cT1-2N0M0) SCLC treated with SBRT and chemotherapy between 2004 and 2020. To assess practice patterns in relation to survival outcomes, patients were categorized into 2 cohorts: "SBRT before chemotherapy" and "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." χ2 tests and logistic regression models were used to determine patient characteristics associated with treatment sequencing. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess the association between patient characteristics and survival outcomes. Overall survival was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via the log-rank test. Sensitivity analyses were performed using multivariable logistic regressions and Cox proportional hazards models for treatments with a 30-day overlap and clinical T stage stratification.
RESULTS: Among 631 patients with clinical stage I SCLC who were treated with SBRT and chemotherapy, 416 (65.9%) were categorized in "SBRT before chemotherapy" and 215 (34.1%) in "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." Patients diagnosed after 2018 were less likely to receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy (odds ratio, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.32-0.66; P < .001). Patients diagnosed with clinical stage T2 were more likely to receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy (odds ratio, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.05-2.95; P = .03). No statistically significant difference in survival was observed between the 2 treatment sequencing cohorts ("SBRT before chemotherapy": median, 40.5 months vs "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy": median, 35.6 months; log-rank P = .30). On multivariable analysis, SBRT sequencing was not associated with overall survival (hazard ratio = 1.11; P = .35; 95% CI, 0.89-1.37).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that there is no statistically significant difference in survival outcomes for patients who receive SBRT before chemotherapy compared with those who receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy. Therefore, flexibility in treatment sequencing may be appropriate in this population.

title: Lung Multidisciplinary Team Decision-Making Challenges in Perioperative NSCLC: Borderline Resectability and Discordant Responses Through the Lens of Real-World Scenarios.
authors: Cortinovis DL, Canova S, Abbate MI et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Resectable or potentially resectable stage II-III NSCLC encompasses heterogeneous clinical scenarios. The introduction of neoadjuvant and perioperative strategies has expanded treatment options while increasing the complexity of multidisciplinary decision-making and the need to reassess treatment pathways over time.
METHODS: We conducted a single-centre retrospective descriptive analysis of 101 patients with clinical or pathological stage II-III NSCLC discussed within our thoracic multidisciplinary team (MDT) between 2023 and 2025. Using MDT meeting records supplemented by medical records, we analysed decision-making trajectories and the main reasons for changes in treatment strategy.
RESULTS: Three major decision points emerged: selection of preoperative treatment, reassessment of resectability and operability after preoperative treatment, and postoperative assessment of recurrence risk and feasibility of adjuvant treatment. Treatment pathways were modified according to disease response or progression, surgical feasibility, comorbidities, treatment-related toxicity, pathological findings, and postoperative recovery. Particularly challenging scenarios included heterogeneous stage II disease, borderline resectability, and discordant responses after induction therapy.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative management of stage II-III NSCLC requires dynamic, longitudinal multidisciplinary decision-making rather than a single treatment decision at diagnosis. Integrated reassessment of clinical, pathological, and molecular disease characteristics, treatment response, patient fitness, and surgical feasibility may help individualise treatment pathways.

title: Evaluation of the Diagnostic and Prognostic Potential, and Correlation with the Tumor Immune Microenvironment of a Six-miRNA Signature Associated with Platinum Sensitivity in Patients with Early-Stage Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Mortoglou M, Papadaki C, Boukouris AE et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a standard-of-care treatment for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet its efficacy is influenced by multiple factors, such as the functionality of DNA damage response pathways. DNA-damaging agents, like cisplatin, contribute to the generation of an "inflamed" tumor microenvironment (TME), which in turn correlates with an active antitumor immune response. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a family of small, non-coding RNAs, have emerged as critical post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, playing vital roles in modulating DNA Damage Repair (DDR) pathways and sensitivity to cisplatin. Their functional involvement in these mechanisms underscores their potential as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in lung cancer.
METHODS: In this study, we investigated the diagnostic and prognostic value of a previously validated six-miRNA signature (hsa-miR-26a, hsa-miR-29c, hsa-miR-34a, hsa-miR-30-5p, hsa-miR-30e-3p and hsa-miR-497) in paired tumor and healthy tissue samples from surgically treated NSCLC patients (n = 76), who later received platinum-based therapy. To explore the translational applicability of this signature, we also compared miRNA expression levels between matched tumor tissue and plasma samples (n = 36). We further examined the presence of an "inflamed" TME and its association with the miRNA signature by examining the mRNA levels of TIGIT, CD8A, FOXP3, CXCL10 and PD-L1, and performing correlation analysis.
RESULTS: All selected miRNAs were significantly downregulated in NSCLC tumor tissue compared to healthy samples. Moreover, miRNA expression was differentially regulated in plasma samples, supporting their potential clinical relevance as minimally invasive biomarkers. The complete six-miRNA signature demonstrated good discriminatory ability between tumor and matched non-malignant tissue (AUC = 0.786, 95% CI: 0.713-0.860; p < 0.001), with 72% sensitivity and 77.3% specificity. A significant correlation with relapse-free survival (RFS) (p = 0.039) was also observed. Distinct immune-related transcriptional alterations were observed in tumor tissue, including increased expression of immune checkpoint-associated genes (TIGIT and PD-L1) and reduced CD8A expression. Tumor PD-L1 expression showed modest positive correlations with miR-26a (p = 0.046) and miR-30e-3p (p = 0.031).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings underscore the potential value of this novel six-miRNA signature both as a prognostic and diagnostic biomarker in NSCLC. Its correlation with immune microenvironment characteristics supports its relevance in guiding personalized therapeutic strategies. This signature warrants further clinical validation and may serve as a valuable tool for patient stratification and outcome prediction for patients treated with platinum-based chemotherapy.

title: Prior splenectomy as a potential risk factor for severe immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated kidney injury: a case report.
authors: Yu Y, Zeng D
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Among immune-related adverse events (irAEs) associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), skin and gastrointestinal toxicities are more frequently observed, whereas severe renal impairment remains uncommon.
CASE PRESENTATION: We herein report a case of immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated acute kidney injury (ICPi-AKI) in a 59-year-old Chinese male with lung squamous cell carcinoma and a history of splenectomy, occurring within two weeks after the first administration of tislelizumab. The patient was managed with intravenous methylprednisolone, intermittent hemodialysis, and subsequent continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), resulting in gradual normalization of serum creatinine levels. Notably, this patient had previously undergone splenectomy. It is postulated that splenectomy may increase the risk of irAEs following ICI therapy, potentially through excessive activation of effector T (Teff) cells.
CONCLUSION: Heightened vigilance is warranted regarding the potential for severe immunotherapy-related toxicity in lung cancer patients with a prior history of splenectomy. For such cases, empirical high-dose glucocorticoids and supportive care-including renal replacement therapy when indicated-is strongly advised.

title: Blocking aryl hydrocarbon receptor remodels myeloid-T cell crosstalk and enhances anti-PD-1 response in the tumor microenvironment.
authors: Kim DK, Baek S, Kim Y et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Cancer metabolism-associated immune suppression remains a major barrier to durable therapeutic responses. Indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 has been pursued as a therapeutic target, but incomplete pathway suppression has limited clinical success. As the aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor and downstream effector of tryptophan metabolism, we investigated how myeloid-cell aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling shapes the tumor immune microenvironment and whether its inhibition can restore antitumor immunity.
METHODS: Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor knockout mice targeting dendritic cells or macrophages were used to evaluate the effects of genetic aryl hydrocarbon receptor ablation. Pharmacologic inhibition was assessed using DA-4505 across syngeneic lung, colorectal, and breast cancer models and an immune checkpoint inhibitor-refractory humanized patient-derived xenograft model. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated alone or in combination with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 therapy, chemotherapy, or surgery. Tumor growth, survival, metastasis, and immune remodeling were analyzed by flow cytometry, multiplex immunohistochemistry, single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and human tumor datasets.
RESULTS: Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor depletion in macrophages and dendritic cells enhanced innate and adaptive immune activation, increased interferon-γ-producing T cells, and strengthened antitumor immunity. In mouse tumor models, pharmacologic aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade enhanced macrophage chemotaxis and activation programs, promoted M1-like macrophage polarization, increased interferon-γ-producing CD8⁺ T cells, and reduced regulatory T cells and polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells. These changes promoted robust T-cell activation and durable tumor control. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition further synergized with chemotherapy, surgery, and immune checkpoint blockade, leading to expansion of effector and memory T-cell populations and sustained antitumor responses. In a humanized lung cancer model, aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade increased intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic-memory programs while reducing regulatory T-cell enrichment. In human tumor datasets, aryl hydrocarbon receptor-positive macrophages correlated with FOXP3⁺ T-cell infiltration, and higher aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition-associated T-cell signatures were associated with improved patient survival.

title: A Phase I Study of HS-20093 Injection in Combination Therapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
summary: This is a multicenter, open-label, Phase 1 clinical study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HS-20093 combination therapy in subjects with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer without actionable genomic alterations.

title: Association of the MMP12 rs652438 Variant with Lung Cancer Susceptibility: A Smoking-Stratified Analysis.
authors: Shen TC, Chen GL, Hang LW et al.
abstract: Background: Matrix metalloproteinase 12 (MMP12) participates in extracellular-matrix remodeling and smoking-related pulmonary inflammation. This study evaluated the associations of MMP12 rs2276109 and rs652438 with lung cancer susceptibility in a Taiwanese population and examined rs652438 according to smoking status. Materials and Methods: This case-control study included 358 patients with histologically confirmed lung cancer and 716 age- and sex-matched cancer-free controls. Genotypes were determined using polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated under genotype, dominant, recessive, and allele models. Smoking-stratified estimates were adjusted for age and sex. Results: rs2276109 was not associated with lung cancer susceptibility. For rs652438, the CC genotype was associated with higher odds of lung cancer than the TT genotype (OR = 4.68, 95% CI = 2.00-10.99, p = 0.0003). Associations were also observed under the recessive (OR = 4.41, 95% CI = 1.89-10.32) and dominant (OR = 1.51, 95% CI = 1.12-2.03) models. The C allele was associated with higher lung cancer odds (OR = 1.62, 95% CI = 1.25-2.11). Among ever-smokers, the CC genotype remained associated with lung cancer after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR = 5.63, 95% CI = 2.17-15.38), whereas no significant association was observed among non-smokers. Conclusions:MMP12 rs652438, but not rs2276109, was associated with lung cancer susceptibility in this Taiwanese population. The association was more apparent among ever-smokers, although formal genotype-smoking interaction analyses were not statistically significant. Independent replication and functional investigation are warranted.

title: Hypoxia-Driven Extracellular Vesicle Signaling in Lung Cancer Progression, Immune Evasion, and Therapeutic Resistance.
authors: Mirbabaei Ghafghazi D, Klentrou P, Sze SK et al.
abstract: Tumor hypoxia is a defining feature of solid tumors, including lung cancer, and a major driver of aggressive disease progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Although hypoxia-induced signaling is well-characterized at the cellular level, emerging evidence highlights extracellular vesicles (EVs) as critical mediators through which hypoxic tumor cells remodel the tumor microenvironment. EVs transfer proteins, nucleic acids, and metabolites between cells, enabling complex intercellular communication. Their diverse cargo can act synergistically to promote cancer progression by modulating multiple signaling pathways in recipient cells. In lung cancer, hypoxia enhances EV biogenesis and promotes the loading of oncogenic cargo. Hypoxia-conditioned EVs subsequently drive key cancer hallmarks, including angiogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metabolic reprogramming, immune suppression, and therapeutic resistance. Despite the diversity of EV cargo, these effects converge on major oncogenic pathways, including PI3K-Akt, STAT3, Wnt/β-catenin, and PD-1/PD-L1 signaling. Therefore, targeting hypoxia-driven EV signaling may suppress tumor progression and improve treatment efficacy. Clinically, the hypoxia-EV axis offers diagnostic and therapeutic opportunities. Circulating EVs containing hypoxia-associated tumor signatures may support non-invasive liquid biopsy approaches for early detection, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Targeting EV biogenesis or transfer may also help overcome resistance to targeted therapy and immunotherapy.

title: Expanding the Value of Lung Cancer Screening through Skeletal Risk Assessment.
authors: Bredella MA

title: Circulating Tumour Cell GALNT13 Expression Is Associated with Prognosis and Treatment Response in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Fernández Armúa E, Serrano MJ, Santana D et al.
abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach to identify clinically informative tumour-derived markers. Given the emerging role of GalNAc-transferases in cancer biology, we evaluated GALNT13 expression in peripheral blood as a potential biomarker for prognosis and disease monitoring in lung cancer patients. Sensitive molecular assays (nested and digital RT-PCR) were developed to detect GALNT13 mRNA in circulating tumour cells (CTCs).
