These methods were applied to peripheral blood samples from non-small cell lung cancer patients to assess prognostic value and enable longitudinal monitoring. A cohort of 143 NSCLC patients was analysed, of whom 60% were GALNT13-positive in peripheral blood at baseline. During a five-year follow-up, GALNT13 positivity was significantly associated with reduced overall survival. In several patients, increases in GALNT13 levels preceded radiologic evidence of disease progression. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

title: FragMIL: A Fragment-Token Multiple-Instance Learning Framework for Cancer Detection from Cell-Free DNA Fragmentomics.
authors: Bui TD, Lin YF, Nguyen MH et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentomics from low-coverage whole-genome sequencing (lcWGS) is a promising approach for non-invasive cancer detection. However, most existing methods summarize millions of cfDNA fragments into handcrafted sample-level features before classification, potentially discarding informative patterns carried by individual molecules. We aimed to develop and benchmark a framework that learns directly from fragment-level signals. Methods: We developed FragMIL, a fragment-token multiple-instance learning framework that represents each cfDNA molecule as a learnable token integrating end-motif, genomic-position, and fragment-length information, and aggregates thousands of fragment tokens into a patient-level cancer score. FragMIL was evaluated on 934 samples from three public lcWGS cohorts (pan-cancer, lung cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma) using five repeated subject-level splits, a 288-configuration design-space benchmark, and comparison with four established fragmentomic approaches (coverage, DELFI, end motif, and fragment size). Results: FragMIL achieved the highest mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) in every cohort, with 0.963 ± 0.009, 0.802 ± 0.009, and 0.910 ± 0.015 in the DELFI/Cristiano 2019, LUCAS/Mathios 2021, and Jiang 2015 cohorts, respectively. End-motif encoding provided the strongest standalone discriminative signal, whereas the optimal fragment pool was cohort-dependent, with open chromatin region fragments performing best for pan-cancer detection and tumor-enriched fragments for disease-specific cohorts. Performance was retained across cancer stages and cancer types. Conclusions: Preserving molecule-level fragmentomic information improves cancer detection, supporting fragment-token learning as a promising framework for next-generation cfDNA fragmentomics.

title: Surgical outcomes of patients with multifocal ground-glass opacities of the lungs located in the same pulmonary lobe.
authors: Komori K, Hattori A, Fukui M et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Multifocal ground-glass opacities (GGOs) detected on thin-section computed tomography are occasionally located in the same pulmonary lobe with multiple expressions and appropriate treatment strategies have not been established.
METHODS: We reviewed cases involving surgically resected multifocal GGOs located in the same pulmonary lobe from 2010 to 2016. "Multifocal" was defined as three or more tumors in the same lobe with or without additional tumors in other lobes, while "GGO" was a tumor that showed pure-GGO or part-solid appearance on radiological imaging. The clinicopathological factors and prognosis were compared between patients with multifocal GGOs (Group M, n = 54) and those with a single GGO (Group N, n = 872).
RESULTS: The median number of tumors in the same lobe was 6 (range 3-38). After a median follow-up period of 7 years, the 5/10-year overall survival (5/10-year OS) of group M was almost equivalent to that of group N (94.3/90.7% versus 94.6/89.1%, p = 0.866). According to the surgical procedure for group M, there was no significant difference in the 5/10-year overall survival rate for either sublobar resection or lobectomy (96.2/96.2% versus 88.9/88.9%, p = 0.380).
CONCLUSION: Multifocal GGOs located in the same pulmonary lobe carry a good prognosis, comparable to a single GGO. Surgical intervention, including sublobar resection, would likely yield an acceptable outcome.

title: Closed-form elasticity and elementary-effect sensitivity analysis of the universal survival curve model for stereotactic radiotherapy fractionation.
authors: Singh A, Singh RK
abstract:
PURPOSE: The universal survival curve (USC) joins the linear-quadratic (LQ) description of the shoulder region to the log-linear multi-target asymptote at a transition dose, and is increasingly invoked to justify ablative fractionation. Which input actually controls predicted survival has not been established analytically. We derive closed-form elasticities, rank the inputs by two independent methods, and quantify the consequences for stereotactic schedules.
METHODS: Continuity of value and gradient at the transition dose fixes the quadratic coefficient and the transition dose in terms of the three cell-line parameters. Elasticities were derived in closed form, verified against central differences, and ranked independently by Morris elementary-effect screening over a fifteen per cent envelope. Biologically effective doses were compared for six clinical schedules and nine non-small-cell lung cancer cell lines.
RESULTS: Dose dominated, with mean absolute elasticity 7.89, followed by the mean inactivation dose 6.64, the quasi-threshold dose 1.15 and the radiosensitivity coefficient 0.104. Morris screening reproduced this ordering. The two agreed for conventional fractionation but diverged sharply above the transition dose, the LQ formulation overstating biologically effective dose by 42 per cent for 54 Gy in three fractions and by 97 per cent for a single 30 Gy fraction.
CONCLUSION: Within the USC model and the in vitro data examined, predicted survival is governed by delivered dose and the characteristic dose rather than by the radiosensitivity coefficient, so parameter-estimation effort should target the terminal slope of the survival curve; the analysis ranks the inputs of each model but does not adjudicate between the models.

title: What Does Standard 5.8 Measure? Nodal Adequacy as an Accountability Metric in Lung Cancer Surgery.
authors: Androutsopoulou V, Zotos PA, Abbaker N et al.
abstract: This unstructured narrative review appraises lymph node evaluation as an accountability measure in non-small cell lung cancer surgery. Commission on Cancer Operative Standard 5.8 requires assessment of at least three mediastinal and one hilar nodal station for every curative-intent resection, with accreditation consequences. We ask what the standard has been validated to measure, and at which level of attribution. Neither the count-based nor the station-based threshold was derived from interventional evidence. The reported value reflects surgeon technique, surgeon-led specimen process, pathologist effort, operative platform, and case mix together, which bears on attribution to individual surgeons rather than on the legitimacy of the measure. We separate two causal models linking nodal evaluation to survival and examine each against evidence identified by a reproducible search, including the biomarker-directed and neoadjuvant eras and sublobar resection. Anchored to the National Quality Forum and Donabedian criteria, we conclude that Standard 5.8 is well-supported as an institutional minimum standard for staging completeness, that the evidence identified does not yet support extension to individual-surgeon benchmarking, that compliance should be reported stratified by resection type, and that low sublobar compliance most plausibly identifies a real quality problem. Nothing here reduces the obligation to perform systematic nodal assessment.

title: Complications of Percutaneous Thermal Ablation of Primary and Metastatic Lung Tumors: Review of Prevention and Management Strategies.
authors: How GY, Pua U
abstract: Pulmonary malignancies encompassing both primary lung cancer and metastatic lesions are a leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally. Percutaneous thermal ablation of primary and metastatic lung tumors using radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation, or cryoablation has emerged as an established minimally invasive treatment modality for selected patients unsuitable for surgery or requiring lung preservation. Although most lung ablation complications are self-limiting, some adverse events may result in long-term morbidity or mortality. Post-ablation pneumothorax has the highest reported incidence, with pooled incidences of 37-44%, although rates may vary according to patient cohorts and study definitions. As indications for percutaneous thermal ablation of pulmonary lesions expand to include complex lesions or higher-risk patients, the prevention and management of procedure-related complications remain central to safe clinical practice. Although prior reviews have described the techniques, oncological outcomes, and complication profiles of image-guided lung ablation, less emphasis has been placed on integrating practical complication prevention and management strategies throughout the periprocedural workflow. This narrative review aims to synthesize various complication prevention and management strategies for percutaneous thermal ablation of both primary and metastatic pulmonary lesions. The review focuses on both common and rare complications, and various aspects of complication prevention such as patient/lesion selection, procedural planning, and anesthesia/respiratory control. A comprehensive understanding of complication profiles and mitigation strategies is essential to optimize procedural safety, guide patient selection, and establish ablative techniques as a pillar in multidisciplinary thoracic oncology care.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
authors: Chen W, Yang F, Zeng F et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: During lung cancer radiotherapy, inter-fractional anatomical changes may cause the delivered dose to deviate from the primary plan, affecting tumor control and increasing the risk of normal tissue damage. This study aims to evaluate the impact of anatomical changes on the dosimetric and radiobiological performance of simulated proton arc therapy (sPAT) versus intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) for lung cancer patients under patient-specific anatomical changes.
METHODS: Data from 21 lung cancer patients were retrospectively analyzed. The prescribed dose for all patients was 6000 cGy (relative biological effectiveness, RBE). Each patient with a primary planning computed tomography (pCT) and a mid-treatment adaptive-planning CT (aCT) acquired at a median of 29 days into treatment due to notable tumor volume changes. Primary plans for sPAT and IMPT were designed on the pCT. After rigid registration of the pCT and aCT, non-adaptive plans (sPATp-a, IMPTp-a) were generated by directly recalculating the doses of the primary plans on the aCT. The comparison evaluated the dosimetric impact of anatomical changes by comparing non-adaptive plans (sPATp-a vs. IMPTp-a). Dose-volume histogram (DVH) parameters for targets and organs at risk (OARs) and tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) were evaluated.
RESULTS: For the primary plans, sPAT and IMPT achieved similar target coverage, while the doses to OARs were generally lower in sPATp. Under anatomical changes, both non-adaptive plans exhibited a decrease in target coverage, sPATp-a achieved a D95% of 5567.57 cGy[RBE] compared with 5423.33 cGy[RBE] for IMPTp-a (p < 0.001), indicating that sPAT better preserved target coverage. Compared with the primary plans, sPATp-a and IMPTp-a exhibited TCP reductions of 5.83% and 8.07%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with IMPT, sPAT exhibits enhanced robustness against inter-fractional anatomical changes occurring in lung-cancer radiotherapy.

title: Thoracoscopic lobectomy for a mediastinal basal pulmonary artery: a case highlighting the importance of pulmonary arterial variations.
authors: Toyohara K, Okai S, Takeda S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mediastinal basal pulmonary artery (MPA) variations may increase the risk of unintentional vascular division or excessive bleeding during pulmonary resection. Therefore, precise preoperative anatomical assessment is particularly important.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a rare case of a MPA that was precisely identified preoperatively using three-dimensional computed tomography (3D-CT). Preoperative three-dimensional CT clearly demonstrated an independently branching mediastinal basal pulmonary artery. The patient underwent thoracoscopic left lower lobectomy for primary lung cancer. MPA branched independently from the main pulmonary artery, and division at the ventral interlobar level resulted in the formation of a relatively long arterial stump. The procedure was completed safely without unintentional vascular division, excessive bleeding, or postoperative thrombotic complications.
CONCLUSION: Previous reports have described interlobar division of anomalous pulmonary arteries in similar cases. However, the clinical benefit of additional proximal dissection solely to shorten the pulmonary artery stump remains unclear. Unnecessary dissection may increase the risk of bleeding. Careful preoperative anatomical assessment using 3D-CT enables safe surgical management. With expanding indications for segmentectomy, accurate recognition of pulmonary arterial variations will become increasingly important in clinical practice.

title: Using an Artificial Intelligence Software Tool (iSeg) During Radiation Treatment Planning for Patients With Lung Tumors
conditions: Metastatic Malignant Neoplasm in the Lung
summary: This clinical trial studies whether an artificial intelligence (AI) software tool called iSeg can be safely and effectively used during routine radiation treatment planning for patients with lung tumors. Typical radiation treatment planning involves physicians manually outlining the tumors to plan where the radiation therapy will be delivered. This process can be time consuming and may vary between physicians. iSeg uses AI to analyze computed tomography (CT) images and generate a proposed tumor outline that can then be reviewed and modified by the treating physician during radiation treatment planning which may help improve accuracy and provide more consistent results and better planning. iSeg may be safe and effective to use during radiation treatment planning for patients with lung tumors.

title: Chest Radiotherapy Associated Cardiotoxicity: An Update.
authors: Agarwal R, Gonzales-Uribe AG, Zhang L
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Chest radiotherapy has improved cancer survival in various thoracic malignancies, including breast cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and lung cancer. However, inadvertent radiation exposure to the heart is associated with a broad spectrum of cardiovascular toxicities, collectively termed radiation-induced heart disease (RIHD). We aim to review the pathophysiology of RIHD and the current evidence for their incidence, risk factors, clinical management, and prevention strategies.
RECENT FINDINGS: RIHD is mediated by oxidative stress, DNA damage, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and progressive fibrosis, leading to accelerated atherosclerosis, myocardial stiffening, valvular degeneration, pericardial disease, and arrhythmias. The risk, timing, and severity of cardiovascular complications are influenced by radiation dose and distribution, age at exposure, baseline cardiovascular risk, and concomitant cardiotoxic therapies. While younger patients may experience prolonged latency before clinical disease onset, older individuals and those with pre-existing cardiovascular disease often develop complications earlier, reflecting radiation-mediated acceleration of underlying pathology. This review summarizes the epidemiology, latency, clinical presentation, surveillance strategies, and management of the different forms of RIHD. It also discusses contemporary approaches to risk mitigation, including advances in radiation delivery techniques, aggressive cardiovascular risk factor modification, lifestyle interventions, and emerging pharmacologic strategies.

title: Prioritizing Emergency Medical Conditions for Health Policy Using a Stepwise Treatable-Death Framework: A Nationwide Analysis in Korea, 2018-2022.
authors: Jeongmin M, Yoon C, Hyun JH et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Limited emergency-care resources require priorities based not only on mortality rates or death counts but also on the potential mortality reduction under explicit targets. We applied the age- and sex-standardized domestic short- and mid-term components of a stepwise treatable-death framework across severe emergency conditions in Korea. Methods: This retrospective nationwide study used NEDIS aggregate data from 16 regions during 2018-2022. The 20 conditions with the highest numbers of in-hospital deaths were represented as 17 groups by replacing sepsis (A41), bacterial pneumonia (J15), pneumonia of unspecified organism (J18), and pneumonitis due to solids and liquids (J69) with an extended-sepsis composite. Treatable deaths were the positive difference between observed and target-based expected deaths. National rates in 10-year age-group and sex strata were applied to regional distributions. The short-term target assumed that regions with an age- and sex-standardized mortality ratio (SMR) above 1.0 achieved the national reference level (SMR = 1.0), whereas the mid-term target assumed that all regions achieved the lowest regional SMR for the corresponding condition and year. Five-year cumulative estimates were the primary outcome measure. Results: Across the 17 groups, summed condition-level patient counts totaled 3,384,529 and in-hospital deaths totaled 357,404 (ratio of summed death counts to summed patient counts, 10.56%). Five-year cumulative short-term estimates were highest for extended sepsis (2387), bronchus and lung cancer (1984), and cardiac arrest (1662). Mid-term estimates were highest for cardiac arrest (21,547), extended sepsis (19,340), and severe trauma (7010). Conclusions: After accounting for regional differences in age and sex distributions, extended sepsis remained the condition with the largest short-term and the second-largest mid-term treatable-death burden, supporting its consideration for further policy-priority evaluation. Each treatable-death estimate is an operational policy-scenario estimate rather than an estimate of causally preventable mortality.

title: The Impact of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis on the Incidence and Severity of Radiation Pneumonitis in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients Following Radiotherapy.
authors: Oh BW, Kim HM, Lee GI et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is known to increase the risk of severe pulmonary toxicity in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients undergoing radiotherapy. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of comorbid IPF on the incidence and severity of radiation pneumonitis (RP) and overall survival (OS). Methods: This retrospective cohort study included NSCLC patients who received radiotherapy to the lung between 2015 and 2025. Patients were stratified into an IPF-comorbid group and a non-IPF control group. To minimize selection bias, variable-ratio (up to 1:2) propensity score matching with a caliper of 0.2 SD and survey-weighted analyses were utilized. Results: After matching, 196 patients (72 with IPF, 124 without IPF) were analyzed. The IPF-comorbid group had a significantly higher risk of any-grade RP (OR = 2.75, p = 0.001) and grade ≥ 2 RP (OR = 2.87, p = 0.002). In multivariable analysis, comorbid IPF was independently associated with any-grade RP (adjusted OR = 3.55, p = 0.001) and grade ≥ 2 RP (adjusted OR = 3.79, p = 0.001). With death as a competing event, the 6-month cumulative incidence of RP was 51.8% vs. 25.2%. IPF was independently associated with worse OS (adjusted HR = 2.51, p = 0.006), with a lower 3-year OS rate (44.4% vs. 68.1%). Conclusions: Comorbid IPF was independently associated with an increased risk of RP and overall mortality in NSCLC patients receiving radiotherapy. Because the cumulative incidence of RP diverged within the first months after radiotherapy, close multidisciplinary monitoring is warranted during this early period.

title: Non-Nodular CT Patterns of Solid Lung Cancer in the Early Growth Phase: A Two-Center Retrospective Study.
authors: Wu XF, Ge XD, Li T et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Early diagnosis of solid lung cancer (SLC) is essential for better prognosis. However, non-nodular patterns, atypical CT manifestations of SLC in the early growth phase, are easily overlooked, potentially leading to delayed diagnosis. This study aimed to characterize the clinical features and CT findings of non-nodular patterns of SLC in the early growth phase. Methods: Between January 2015 and October 2025, 365 patients with 365 pathologically confirmed SLCs were retrospectively enrolled from two centers. Based on initial morphological appearances, lesions were classified into nodular and non-nodular groups (patch-like, strip-like, bead-like, pleural plaque-like, and cystic-cavity subtypes). Clinical data and CT findings were summarized and compared between the two groups. Results: Of the 365 SLCs, 107 (29.32%) initially presented as non-nodular lesions, among which patch-like lesions (56, 52.34%) were the most prevalent, followed by bead-like (20, 18.69%), strip-like (16, 14.95%), pleural plaque-like (9, 8.41%), and cystic-cavity lesions (6, 5.61%). Both nodular and non-nodular lesions were predominantly located in the upper lobes (55.04% vs. 58.88%, p = 0.611). Multivariable analysis revealed that smoking history (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.93; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.05-8.28; p = 0.040), subpleural distribution (aOR, 3.37; 95% CI, 1.61-7.72; p < 0.001), interstitial lung disease (ILD) (aOR, 66.45; 95% CI, 23.57-220.04; p < 0.001), and post-tuberculosis lung changes (aOR, 8.60; 95% CI, 2.37-32.64; p = 0.001) were independently associated with a non-nodular pattern (AUC: 0.869; p < 0.001). Conclusions: In smokers or patients with ILD/post-tuberculosis lung changes, subpleural non-nodular lesions in the upper lobes require close monitoring for growth.

title: Optimising radiotherapy and immunotherapy timing: a mechanistic model of the tumour microenvironment.
authors: Ng AM, D'Alonzo RA, Keam S et al.
abstract: This study aimed to determine the optimal scheduling of radiotherapy (RT) and anti-PD-1/CTLA-4 immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in a murine model of mesothelioma. BALB/c mice inoculated with a syngeneic mesothelioma tumour on the flank were treated with combination RT and ICI, and tumour growth was measured. An extension of an existing mechanistic model of the tumour microenvironment was fitted to the data, estimating growth, clearing of RT-damaged tumour cells, release of antigens, and activation of T-cells. This model was further extended to investigate the effects of tumour hypoxia on treatment efficacy. Each treatment schedule was analysed to calculate the highest tumour control probability (TCP). Combining ICIs with RT increases the TCP, consistent with other pre- clinical studies. Anti-PD-1 was more effective than anti-CTLA-4 at enhancing tumour control in our model. However, administering anti-PD-1 alone was less effective compared to combined anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1. The TCP was robust to changes in the interval between ICI treatment days and delaying anti-CTLA-4 treatment. However, TCP was sensitive to delays in RT treatment and increases in the interval between RT treatment days. This study supports the synergistic effect between RT and ICIs. Further validation of the model on an external dataset is required before the model can be used to inform optimal treatment scheduling for future human clinical trials.

title: AIRE Deficiency Impairs Thymic Epithelial Progenitor Differentiation from Mouse Embryonic Stem Cells and Accelerates Type 1 Diabetes in NOD/Ltj Mice.
authors: Li Y, He K, Qu X et al.
abstract: The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) is essential for central immune tolerance, but its role in thymic epithelial cell (TEC) differentiation and development remains incompletely understood. To address this, we knocked down AIRE in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and analyzed thymic epithelial progenitor (TEP) differentiation using RNA-sequencing and also performed thymic AIRE knockdown in NOD/Ltj mice to evaluate type 1 diabetes (T1D) pathogenesis. AIRE knockdown significantly reduced the proportion of K5+/K8+ TEPs among EpCAM1+ cells and altered the ECM-receptor interaction pathway, with downregulation of SPP1 and upregulation of Fn1 and CD44. Importantly, re-expression of AIRE using an shRNA-resistant rescue vector partially reversed these molecular changes and partially restored TEP differentiation. In vivo, thymic AIRE knockdown accelerated blood glucose elevation, aggravated insulitis, and reduced expression of T1D-associated TSAs (INS2, GAD67) and maturation markers (CD80, MHC-II). Importantly, the changes in SPP1, Fn1, and CD44 were consistent between in vitro and in vivo models. Furthermore, AIRE deficiency increased CD4+ single-positive thymocytes, reduced splenic Treg frequency, and enhanced antigen-specific T cell proliferation and activation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AIRE deficiency impairs TEP differentiation and alters the ECM-receptor pathway, while thymic AIRE deficiency compromises immune tolerance and accelerates T1D progression in NOD/Ltj mice.

title: To Be or Not to Be-Thymocyte Survival and Death in the Thymic Medulla.
authors: Zúñiga MC
abstract: The T cells of the mammalian immune system have a tricky challenge. They must recognize foreign antigen as "other" or "non-self" but in the context of self, while also being tolerant to the body's own molecules and tissues. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement occurs in the cortex of the thymus and generates receptors of relatively random specificity. The developing T cells (thymocytes) are screened in two stages, both of which are Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)-based. The first, positive selection, occurs in the thymic cortex where cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) display self MHC + self-peptides. Thymocytes that can bind to self MHC + self-peptide then migrate to the corticomedullary junction, where they undergo negative selection. Here, they encounter antigenic peptides characteristic of peripheral tissue proteins presented by medullary antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Among the most intriguing APCs in the medulla are the mimetic medullary thymic epithelial cells (mimetic mTECs). These mimetic APCs express peripheral antigens under the direction of specific transcription factors. During negative selection, most thymocytes whose TCRs bind too well to self MHC + self-peptide die by apoptosis. However, a small proportion of autoreactive thymocytes escape negative selection and instead "alternatively" differentiate into specialized cell types that are self-tolerant and even enforce self-tolerance. The CD4 and CD8 coreceptors, which bind to MHC II and MHC I, respectively, play crucial roles in positive and negative selection. With CD8, there is an added level of complexity because there are two forms of CD8, only one of which can promote signaling through the TCR. Upon binding to MHC, CD4 and CD8 initiate signal transduction through the TCR. The strength of signal transduction through the TCR and through co-stimulatory CD28 determines the outcome of TCR-MHC + peptide binding. Signal transduction occurs within the immunological synapse and is regulated by kinetic proofreading mechanisms. In summary, negative selection involves interactions between developing thymocytes and a variety of medullary APCs. These molecular interactions occur at specialized membrane domains that bring together the components of the TCR signaling apparatus, which are subject to kinetic proofreading. Together, the regulatory mechanisms occurring in developing thymocytes and in medullary APCs generate a T-cell arsenal that is tolerant of self and active against foreign entities.

title: Post-Recurrence Treatment Patterns and Outcomes After Curative-Intent Multimodality Strategy in Patients with Pleural Mesothelioma: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Illini O, Fabikan H, Berghammer I et al.
abstract: Background: Disease recurrence is common after surgery for pleural mesothelioma (PM), and the evidence guiding post-recurrence management remains limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-center cohort study including patients with PM treated within a curative-intent multimodality treatment pathway including surgery aiming for a macroscopic complete resection when feasible between 2001 and 2024. Post-recurrence treatments were categorized as best supportive care only (BSC), systemic therapy alone, or local with or without systemic therapy. Survival and disease-free outcomes were analyzed in relation to treatment patterns and clinical prognostic factors. Results: Among 67 patients with a median follow-up time of 107 months from surgery, 58 (86.6%) developed disease recurrence. At first recurrence, 21 patients (36%) received local with or without systemic therapy, 26 (45%) systemic therapy alone, and 11 (19%) BSC. The median post-recurrence survival was 21.7 months for patients receiving local with or without systemic therapy, 10.8 months for systemic therapy alone, and 1.6 months for BSC. Lung-sparing surgery and a disease-free interval of at least 12 months were associated with improved post-recurrence survival and post-recurrence progression-free survival. Conclusions: In this real-world cohort of patients with PM and extended follow-up, active post-recurrence treatment was associated with longer post-recurrence survival in selected patients. However, conclusions regarding their comparative effectiveness are limited by the retrospective design, incomplete recurrence-related data, and patient selection at recurrence.

title: Prognostic Significance of B7-H3, TROP2, and p16 Expression in Pleural Mesothelioma: Clinicopathological Correlations and Survival Outcomes.
authors: Tas N, Yüceer RO, Koc T et al.
abstract: Background: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive malignancy with considerable biological heterogeneity and few established prognostic biomarkers. We evaluated the clinicopathological and prognostic relevance of B7-H3, TROP2, and p16 expression in PM. Methods: This retrospective study included 50 patients with histologically confirmed PM diagnosed between 2016 and 2025. Immunohistochemical expression of B7-H3, TROP2, and p16 was evaluated using an immunoreactivity scoring system. Associations with clinicopathological features were examined, and overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards methods. Results: High B7-H3, TROP2, and p16 expression was observed in 78%, 18%, and 20% of tumors, respectively. High B7-H3 expression was significantly associated with asbestos exposure, chemotherapy, and tumor stage. Patients with high B7-H3 expression had shorter median OS (11.0 vs. 42.0 months; p < 0.001) and PFS (11.0 vs. 40.0 months; p = 0.004) than those with negative/low expression. Neither TROP2 nor p16 expression was significantly associated with survival. In a parsimonious multivariable Cox model, high B7-H3 expression remained significantly associated with poorer OS after adjustment for disease stage (HR = 4.42, 95% CI: 1.29-15.21, p = 0.018). Conclusions: B7-H3 is frequently expressed in PM and was associated with poorer survival, including after adjustment for disease stage. These findings support further investigation of B7-H3 as a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in PM.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics and Machine Learning Unveil Plakophilin 1 as a Robust Diagnostic Biomarker for Thymoma.
authors: Li Y, Zhang S, Gao Q et al.
abstract: Background: Thymoma (THYM) is a rare epithelial tumor originating in the anterior mediastinum. Due to the lack of specific clinical manifestations and reliable molecular biomarkers, its diagnosis and treatment are often delayed until advanced stages. Although multi-omics technologies have provided new strategies for biomarker discovery, systematic integrative studies specifically focused on thymoma remain limited. Objectives: This study aimed to identify and validate potential diagnostic biomarkers for thymoma through the integration of multi-omics data and machine learning approaches. Methods: We integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and epigenomic datasets and applied machine learning algorithms to screen for core candidate genes. The cell-type-specific expression patterns of the identified candidates were further evaluated using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and their potential molecular functions were predicted via in silico perturbation analysis. In addition, immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed to validate the differential expression of the candidate biomarker at the protein level. Results: Six core candidate genes-interferon regulatory factor 6 (IRF6), thyroid hormone receptor interactor 6 (TRIP6), plakophilin 1 (PKP1), cadherin 1 (CDH1), pre-B-cell leukemia transcription factor 1 (PBX1), and keratin 1 (KRT1)-were identified through machine learning. Among these, PKP1 demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance in both the training set (area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, AUC: 0.83; sensitivity: 0.80; specificity: 0.875) and the validation set (AUC: 0.94; sensitivity: 0.93; specificity: 1.000). Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed a significantly enriched expression pattern of PKP1 in thymoma tumor cells. In silico perturbation analysis suggested that PKP1 may be involved in cell adhesion and tumor progression through regulation of the extracellular matrix (ECM)-integrin-cytoskeleton axis. Immunohistochemistry further validated the significantly elevated protein expression level of PKP1 in thymoma tissues. Conclusions: This study identifies PKP1 as a potential diagnostic biomarker for thymoma with high diagnostic performance and tumor cell-enriched expression, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying thymoma progression and its potential clinical applications.

title: MTAP Loss and Pleural Mesothelioma (PM): Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches.
authors: Cedres S, Masfarre L, Priano I et al.
abstract: PM is a locally aggressive tumor associated with asbestos exposure. Despite legislative efforts to regulate asbestos use, its incidence continues to rise in some parts of the world. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy have improved survival in PM patients, but overall survival remains poor. MTAP loss is frequent in PM and may influence tumor behavior, resulting in a poorer prognosis. MTAP-deficient tumors exhibit unique metabolic vulnerabilities that have stimulated the development of targeted therapeutic strategies in recent years with promising results. The aim of this review is to analyze the prognostic and predictive value of MTAP in PM patients, as well as the outcomes of drugs with potential activity against this target.

title: Primum Non Nocere: Ethical Considerations of Cytoreductive Surgery and Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (CRS/HIPEC) in Peritoneal Malignancies.
authors: Williams JK, Wong W, Viana SW et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (CRS/HIPEC) offers survival benefit for select patients with peritoneal surface malignancies (PSMs), yet the ethical dimensions of patient selection, informed consent, and multidisciplinary care remain underexplored. In a field still evolving, where patients with comparable profiles may exhibit vastly different prognoses, a structured ethical framework can serve as a compass for surgical decision-making.
METHODS: A narrative review of the literature examined the ethical considerations surrounding CRS/HIPEC for PSM. Topics include patient selection, the biological spectrum from indolent to aggressive disease, technical feasibility of complete cytoreduction, shared decision-making, surgical morbidity, palliative care integration, and special populations.
RESULTS: The strength of evidence supporting CRS/HIPEC varies substantially by tumor biology, from near-curative outcomes in low-grade appendiceal neoplasms to marginal benefit in aggressive histologies such as sarcomatoid mesothelioma and signet ring cell carcinoma. When complete cytoreduction cannot be achieved, the procedure is unlikely to confer meaningful survival benefit and may cause significant harm. Traditional informed consent often omits the elements of informed decision-making; structured frameworks such as Best Case/Worst Case and REMAP (Reframe, Expect emotion, Map values, Align, Propose a plan) can bridge this gap. Decision regret data suggest that inadequate preoperative expectation setting contributes to patient dissatisfaction independent of surgical outcomes. Early palliative care and multidisciplinary collaboration improve prognostic understanding and alignment of treatment with patient goals.
CONCLUSIONS: The ethical principles presented here are not rigid boundaries but flexible guides to help surgeons navigate clinical uncertainty. Although they focus on the surgical decision, they extend to every member of the multidisciplinary team caring for patients with PSM.

title: CT-guided iodine-125 brachytherapy for advanced thymic epithelial tumors: a preliminary observational study.
authors: Tang Z, Qiu S, Liao Y et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to provide a preliminary description of the application of CT-guided iodine-125 (125I) seed implantation, a form of brachytherapy, in patients with advanced or recurrent thymic epithelial tumors (TETs).
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed seven patients with advanced or recurrent TETs who underwent CT-guided 125I seed implantation. Based on the extent of disease at presentation, one patient had widespread distant metastases, while the remaining six had localized lesions. Treatment planning was performed using a treatment planning system(TPS, Beijing Astro Technology Co., Ltd.) with a prescribed dose of 60-70 Gy. Follow-up evaluations included regular contrast-enhanced CT scans. Tumor response was assessed according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, and safety was evaluated using CTCAE v5.0.
RESULTS: A total of 12 lesions were treated across seven patients. All procedures were technically successful. Over a median follow-up of 46 months (range: 9-69 months),four patients (57.1%) attained a complete response (CR) and three patients (42.9%) attained a partial response (PR) at the patient level. Patient-level response was defined by composite assessment of all target lesions. At the lesion level, six lesions (50%) demonstrated a CR and six lesions (50%) demonstrated a partial response PR. Notably, lesion-level observations are statistically non-independent given that half of treated lesions derived from a single patient. Complications included pneumothorax in three patients (one of whom required drainage) and grade 1 radiation pneumonitis in one patient; all adverse events resolved without long-term sequelae. No severe radiation-related toxicities (e.g., pericarditis) were observed. In a descriptive subgroup excluding the patient with widespread metastases, four of six patients achieved CR and two achieved PR; no local progression was documented during available follow-up, but this finding remains descriptive and non-comparative.
CONCLUSION: CT-guided ¹²⁵I radioactive seed implantation appears feasible and well-tolerated in patients with advanced or recurrent TETs. The observed objective tumour responses and toxicity profile are hypothesis-generating but must be interpreted with caution given the very small sample size, heterogeneous cohort, non-independent lesion-level data, and lack of a control group. This preliminary study cannot establish durable local control or superiority over external beam radiotherapy. Further larger, prospective studies with standardized dosimetry and time-to-event endpoints are warranted.

title: Lymphoma response to chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy is driven by endogenous tumor-reactive CD8⁺ T cells
summary: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy induces durable remissions in a subset of patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma; however, most patients fail to respond or eventually relapse. By integrating whole-genome and transcriptome profiling of 54 patients with functional assays, syngeneic models, and mathematical modeling, we demonstrate that durable CAR-T efficacy requires cooperation between CAR-T cells and endogenous CD8 (eCD8) T cells recruited to join the attack on malignant cells. Tumors with biallelic loss of MHC class I or CD58 exhibited high genomic complexity, increased neoantigen burden, and resistance to CAR-T therapy. MHC-I-deficient lymphomas showed suboptimal response in immunocompetent hosts compared to wild type. Importantly, sustained responses in mice occurred only in the presence of eCD8 cells, whereas all CD8-depleted mice relapsed after initial CAR-T-mediated tumor regression. Patients and murine ELISPOT assays confirmed enhanced endogenous T-cell activation post-CAR-T. These findings reveal that CAR-T therapy functions not only as a cytotoxic modality but also as a catalyst for endogenous anti-tumor immunity.
